## [Study: LLM and Rule Gates for Agent Actions Fail Dependently](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07359) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper empirically tests whether deterministic rule layers and LLM-based judges used as runtime gates for agent tool calls fail independently, analyzing 1,119 labeled agent actions from three corpora. It finds that any two LLM judges compose to only about 1.2 to 1.4 multiplication-equivalent layers, while a rule layer plus one judge composes to about 1.86 to 2.09 layers, contradicting the common assumption that gate errors multiply. The findings challenge a foundational assumption in AI agent safety architecture — that stacking independent gates multiplies their error-reduction power — and suggest that adding more LLM judges yields diminishing returns. This has direct implications for how developers design runtime guardrails, budget safety layers, and evaluate agent reliability in production systems. Under the STRICT miss definition (escalation to a human scored as not stopped), six of six judge pairs were statistically significant with a median phi of +0.430, while zero of four rule-plus-judge combinations were significant (median phi +0.014). Solo accuracy did not predict what a layer adds — a cloud rule pack cut the rule layer's solo miss rate by 20% yet added no new joint coverage — and one judge tier was served by an unrequested model version in 50 of 112 batches, overturning a pre-declared analysis rule and reversing five conclusions.

## [Formal Framework Makes AI Agent Claims Auditable Under EU AI Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07459) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07459) proposes a formal definition of "auditable claims" about AI agents, requiring each claim to name its policy, scope, records, and decision rule before any verdict is issued. It extends the Policy Checkability dimension of the Auditable Agents framework from single actions to broader claims, adding three agent-specific conditions: coverage by an independent record, authorization bound to each action's arguments, and completeness beyond integrity. This work directly addresses EU AI Act Article 12, which mandates automatic event logging for high-risk systems but does not specify which records settle a given claim, leaving a critical compliance gap. By providing formal proofs and a claim-check table anchored in NIST, IETF, and OWASP drafts, it offers researchers, auditors, and operators a rigorous method for agent accountability in regulated environments. The framework adapts the preconditions of an assurance engagement, calling a claim auditable when its elements and decision rule are fixed before any verdict and the records are obtainable. Under an explicit model, the authors prove that support is impossible without each of the three agent conditions wherever its hypotheses hold, and they demonstrate the method on six common claims through a worked case spanning five evidence states.

A new arXiv paper introduces COMPASS, an inference-time steering method that uses the correctness of a model's own direct answer attempts as a signal to find a latent 'correctness direction' in attention head activations. By identifying a small subset of heads via a logit-space attribution score and steering their activations along this direction, COMPASS improves GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points on average across three model families and multiple math benchmarks. This work shows that eliciting reasoning may not require complex predefined characterizations like chain-of-thought prompts or sparse autoencoder features, potentially simplifying how practitioners control LLM reasoning at inference time. It also suggests reasoning behavior is concentrated in remarkably few attention heads, which could inform both interpretability research and efficient model steering. COMPASS requires only per-head activation statistics, approaches chain-of-thought accuracy with 20-70% fewer generated tokens, and its interventions transfer to unseen benchmarks without re-fitting. Ablations confirm that both the correctness direction and the small set of heads carrying it are necessary, with the effect concentrated in remarkably few heads.

## [Muon's Flat Spectrum May Suffice: BulkBoost Two-Band Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07497) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07497) analyzes the Muon optimizer's spectral properties and finds that roughly 94–97% of measured singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with a reference gradient. It introduces BulkBoost, a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants, where the latter uses split-minibatch gradient differences and a Marchenko–Pastur reference edge to separate the bulk from the spikes. The results suggest that useful departures from Muon's flat spectral profile are surprisingly low-dimensional, meaning a single bulk-to-spike gain can capture at least as much benefit as fine-grained spectral profiles like Freon. This could simplify optimizer design for large language model training and challenge the trend of increasingly complex per-mode spectral shaping. Across 30 continued-pretraining settings from Pythia-14M to 410M and six corpora, the two-band variants reduce final loss by 0.073–0.147% of the pre-adaptation loss on average, compared with 0.022% for Freon, while outperforming Spectra. The theory provides a first-order condition for when moving weight toward the bulk lowers the loss and quantifies how much of the maximal first-order improvement rate two bands can capture.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Muon is an optimizer for hidden-layer matrix parameters that orthogonalizes the momentum matrix via a polar update Q = UV^T, giving every singular direction equal weight — a property called the flat profile. Recent optimizers such as Freon and Spectra replace this flat profile with fine-grained spectral maps that assign each direction its own gain. The Marchenko–Pastur distribution describes the eigenvalue spectrum of pure noise in random matrices, and its edge is used here to distinguish noise-dominated bulk modes from signal spikes.

## [MARS: Multi-resolution Adaptive Routing for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07505) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces MARS, a multi-resolution user memory for long-history sequential recommendation that writes the full history into recurrent state tracks anchored to different half-lives and uses a sparse routing reader to select relevant temporal resolutions per seed. MARS outperforms strong baselines on three public datasets, with gains that grow with history length, at about 1.02× the warm-cache serving latency of its interface-matched baseline for 1,000 candidates per user. The paper identifies and names 'temporal aliasing' — the uneven preservation of short-, medium-, and long-term signals in monolithic cached user memories — a structural limitation affecting long-history recommenders that cache candidate-independent memory to score large candidate pools. By showing that temporal diversity and selective routing each contribute beyond hard-window memories or added capacity, MARS offers a practical direction for improving recommendation quality without sacrificing the fixed-size, low-latency serving that production systems require. MARS maintains fixed-size candidate scoring by materializing compact seed memories through sparse routing, and component-matched ablations with paired tests confirm that temporal diversity and selective routing each add value. The advantage over the interface-matched baseline widens after within-user behavioral shifts, and the overhead is modest at roughly 1.02× warm-cache serving latency for 1,000 candidates per user.

Recurrent state tracks are memory mechanisms that carry information across time steps, and anchoring them to different half-lives lets a model retain signals at multiple time scales. ## [Causal Tracing Reveals Where Vision-Language Models Form Safety Judgments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07514) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces SSU-Bench, a dataset of matched safe and unsafe image-text pairs built via single-item prompt edits or image edits with annotated intended regions, and uses causal tracing to transfer internal states between paired inputs across three vision-language models. It finds that interventions at changed input positions are effective in earlier decoder layers, while interventions at the final input token become effective only in later layers, and that a linear readout of the final-token state predicts the model's own verdict, including incorrect ones. This work offers a mechanistic account of where multimodal safety decisions become readable inside vision-language models, which matters for AI safety and interpretability because it distinguishes a readable model decision from a correct safety judgment. The layer-specific transition it identifies could inform targeted interventions, auditing tools, and defenses for multimodal systems that are increasingly deployed in safety-critical settings. The study uses three vision-language models and two types of counterfactuals—prompt edits and image edits—and shows that directions estimated from other examples produce similar late-layer effects, with cross-model comparisons revealing similar patterns of counterfactual change. A key caveat is that the linear readout predicts the model's own verdict, including incorrect judgments, so readability does not imply correctness.

Mem0 and Graphiti are popular memory layers for AI agents that manage such extracted facts.

The 3W joint scoring mechanism combines semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state to distinguish relevant past states from later revisions, and the latency drop to 7.03 ms comes from reusing dialogue-backbone intermediate representations instead of re-encoding query audio. The paper introduces VisualNoiseQA, a new benchmark where a text-only LLM must solve visual question answering (VQA) problems by iteratively querying a fixed, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) that acts as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, multiple samples are drawn and an empirical uncertainty signal is exposed via self-consistency, allowing the reasoner to decide what to ask next and when to stop; the benchmark contains 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Most existing active reasoning benchmarks assume environmental feedback is trustworthy or add noise without providing a calibrated uncertainty signal, so this work fills a gap by testing how LLMs reason when evidence itself is uncertain. It could inform the design of more robust agents that must operate with unreliable tools and sensors in real-world settings. The benchmark is constructed automatically and scalably: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable are retained. The uncertainty signal is derived from self-consistency across multiple samples, and the setup treats the VLM as a black-box stochastic sensor rather than a component to be fine-tuned.

## [ST-Bench Tests Multi-Agent Systems on Scientific Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07763) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ST-Bench, a benchmark of 100 Earth science data analysis tasks (hydrology, agriculture, wetland methane) expanded into 2,067 expert-validated queries, to test whether LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) outperform single agents on real scientific analysis. Evaluating five recent MAS generation methods under two training protocols against single-agent baselines on the same GPT-5 backbone, nine of ten MAS configurations beat the cheapest single-agent baseline, with the strongest reaching nearly three times its composite score. This is one of the first benchmarks to test multi-agent systems on real scientific data analysis rather than coding, math, or QA tasks with binary success signals, filling a previously untested evaluation gap. It shows MAS specialization yields measurable but conditional benefits, helping researchers and practitioners decide when the extra cost of multi-agent workflows is justified. The performance gain comes mainly from coverage — trained workflows produce realistic numerical metrics on a larger fraction of queries — while metric quality conditional on producing realistic output is comparable to the single-agent baseline. The strongest configuration needs about four times the single-agent inference time, but a more economical workflow captures most of the benefit at less than twice the cost.

## [Persistent Memory Adds Cost Without Accuracy Gains in Multi-Agent LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07782) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A controlled study of a three-tier agent architecture finds that decomposing long-context inference across cooperating agents cuts peak KV cache to 14.3 MiB per query versus 35.5 and 35.3 MiB for single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. However, adding a persistent memory tier that stores and recalls reasoning traces costs +0.368 MiB of peak cache while producing no detectable accuracy change (+0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]) across eight controlled dataset pairs at n=100 per arm. This negative result challenges the common assumption that persistent memory tiers improve multi-agent LLM inference, suggesting that many reported accuracy gains from such ablations may be artifacts of flawed measurement. It has practical implications for system designers deciding whether to invest in memory tiers, and it highlights the need for more rigorous benchmark designs that can actually detect memory benefits. The authors argue the null result is structural: single-question benchmarks supply each item with its own evidence and score it independently, and correctness requires resetting stored traces between conditions, so recall has nothing informative to retrieve. Reaching this conclusion required four measurement corrections—three inflating the apparent benefit and a fourth making an effect of that size look resolvable—none of which were visible in the results table.

**Background**: In large language model inference, the KV cache stores intermediate attention computations to avoid recomputation, and its memory footprint often becomes the bottleneck for long-context tasks. Multi-agent systems attempt to mitigate this by splitting inference across cooperating agents, and many such systems add a persistent memory tier to store and recall reasoning traces across calls, typically validated by an ablation showing accuracy gains. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a related baseline that retrieves external documents at inference time to supplement the model's context.

OOPMAS is a training-free framework that generates both the agent set and the coordination workflow at the granularity of individual queries, rather than producing one fixed workflow per benchmark task. On a mixed-task benchmark spanning code, math, and QA, it achieves 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points, and reaches 92.4% with the strongest of four tested LLM backbones. By adapting agent composition and workflow per query without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, OOPMAS points toward more flexible, deployment-ready multi-agent systems for real-world mixed workloads. Agents are represented as object-oriented class definitions with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state, while workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without any gradient updates or fine-tuning.

## [LLMs Show Stronger Illusory Pattern Perception Than Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07791) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07791) presents the first systematic study of illusory pattern perception in large language models, adapting classic psychological paradigms across three tasks and comparing results directly to human behavior. The authors find that LLMs frequently exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans, and use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) interpretability framework to show that holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation are linked to these illusions. This finding suggests that LLMs may systematically generate spurious inferences and causal narratives from random or ambiguous data, which could undermine their reliability in downstream applications such as decision support, data analysis, and automated reasoning. It also adds a previously underexplored cognitive-like failure mode to the growing literature on AI safety and human-like biases in LLMs. The study adapts classic psychological paradigms to three tasks and finds that models tend to over-associate frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations, and to construct causal narratives from ambiguous events. The mechanistic analysis relies on Sparse Autoencoders to probe internal representations, and the code is publicly available on GitHub.

In a separate multi-turn evaluation, STEPGATE achieves 69.0% trajectory success and 84.0% action success using only 30.0% cloud actions, compared with 48.0%/70.5% local-only, 60.0%/78.2% random escalation, and 57.0%/77.1% query-level routing, while strong-only reaches 82.0% trajectory success at 100% cloud actions. ## [Confidence Reasoning Graphs Estimate LLM Agent Success from One Trajectory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07948) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.07948) introduces Confidence Reasoning Graphs (CRGs), an inference-time framework that estimates the probability an LLM agent successfully completed its task from a single trajectory, without privileged model access or training data. Instead of a single holistic judgment, a CRG starts from the claim that the agent succeeded, decomposes it into contextualized sub-claims grounded in trajectory evidence, estimates confidence for each terminal claim, and aggregates them into an overall confidence estimate. Reliable confidence estimation is a prerequisite for deploying LLM agents in consequential domains, where a system must decide whether to trust an agent's output or intervene. CRGs offer a practical, training-free approach for this problem, which matters for researchers and practitioners working on agent reliability, AI safety, and human-in-the-loop oversight. Across three agentic benchmarks, three backbone models, and three agent frameworks, CRGs reportedly yield better-calibrated confidence and stronger risk-aware decision making than verbalized, sampling-based, and white-box surrogate baselines. The authors also warn that calibration error alone can be misleading, noting a white-box surrogate baseline that appears well calibrated while providing near-chance discrimination, and ablations attribute CRG's gains to claim-level confidence estimation and aggregation rather than graph construction alone.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are systems in which a large language model plans and executes multi-step tasks, often calling tools and interacting with external environments, so evidence about whether they succeeded is spread across many heterogeneous, interdependent steps. Confidence calibration means making an agent's stated or estimated probability of success match its actual success rate, which is hard when frontier models expose limited internal signals, roll-outs are expensive, and training data may be unavailable or quickly outdated. Prior work such as Agentic Confidence Calibration (ACC) and Holistic Trajectory Calibration (HTC) similarly diagnoses entire execution trajectories rather than only final outputs, and this paper extends that line of research with a graph-based, inference-time method.

A new arXiv paper introduces PAIR, a pipeline for constructing user-conditioned application states that lets researchers evaluate the same task across different users, and RePAIR, a reinforcement learning approach that learns from cross-user differences in subgoal outcomes. Testing six agents, the authors found task success varies substantially across users, with subgoal achievement dropping 6.98 to 15.4 percentage points in user-conditioned UI contexts and 8.77 to 22.0 pp for personal targets drawn from each user's own content; RePAIR improved user-conditioned SAR by 5.87 pp, all-success by 7.50 pp, and overall Task SR by 9.42 pp over its supervised fine-tuning parent on unseen users. As mobile GUI agents move toward real-world deployment, they will encounter highly personalized interfaces shaped by each user's history and preferences, so reliability gaps across users directly threaten practical usability. This work provides both a controlled evaluation methodology and initial evidence that explicitly training on cross-user variation can close those gaps, which is valuable for the AI/ML and HCI communities working on agent deployment. The failures in user-conditioned contexts frequently involve the agent selecting another item instead of the intended target, particularly before the target is exposed on screen. RePAIR's gains are measured on unseen users, suggesting the approach generalizes rather than overfitting to the users seen during training.

## [HMED Distills Revision Consequences to Improve Self-Improving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07979) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces HMED (Hindsight Meta-Experience Distillation), a mechanism that re-executes incumbent and revised Meta-Skills from the same restored discovery state so that the effect of a revision can be observed under a shared condition. Each comparison is distilled into a reusable Meta-Experience, allowing even non-retained revisions to contribute a learning signal, and HMED consistently improves Skill discovery across three interactive agent benchmarks and both open- and closed-source models. This addresses a key limitation in existing self-improving agent methods, where branch performance entangles the initial discovery state with the Meta-Skill revision, biasing updates toward revisions that merely benefit from favorable states. By shifting Meta-Skill learning from branch outcomes toward the consequences of changing the improvement process, HMED could make agent self-improvement more reliable and generalizable. HMED revisits the completed event from which a revision originates and re-executes both the incumbent and revised Meta-Skills from the same restored discovery state, distilling each comparison into a structured Meta-Experience record. The approach is evaluated on three interactive agent benchmarks with both open-source and closed-source models, though it remains an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

**Background**: Self-improving agents generate and revise Skills over time, where Task-Skills directly act on task execution while Meta-Skills govern how agents discover and improve future Skills. In reinforcement learning, a trajectory is the path an agent takes through the state space, and prior approaches improve Meta-Skills from observed raw Skill-search trajectories and branch outcomes. HMED builds on this by disentangling the initial discovery state from the revision itself, treating the process that discovers and refines Skills as a learnable object.

The TGA uses a production supervisor/worker architecture with persistent themes, subthemes, and record-level predictions, and its stability advantage held across every corpus size and when theme matching was made stricter or looser. Researchers from Illuin Technology present DAEDALUS, a method that bootstraps reusable agent memory from self-generated practice tasks without any pre-existing task set or oracle verifier. It pairs an explorer agent that generates challenging yet solvable tasks with a solver agent whose failures yield heuristics, which are accepted only after repeated in-context success and then consolidated into a memory bank. This addresses a core bottleneck in LLM agent research: agents typically need human-written guidelines or oracle verifiers to build procedural memory, both of which require prior environment knowledge. By removing that dependency, DAEDALUS points toward more autonomous agents that can adapt to unfamiliar environments on their own, potentially lowering the cost of deploying agents in new domains. Across AppWorld, τ²-bench, and AutomationBench, DAEDALUS improves mean success rates by up to 15.9 points and pass^5 by up to 2.2x over a no-memory baseline, while remaining competitive with methods that use training tasks at lower inference cost. Ablations show solver traces are the key signal for deriving effective heuristics, and the generated tasks can even serve as a proxy benchmark for ranking models.

QRAKEN, a training-free and ontology-agnostic neurosymbolic pipeline, grounds LLM-based Text-to-SPARQL generation in empirical graph evidence via an offline distiller that produces TTQL—a compact description of populated multi-hop patterns, conditional frequencies, path-conditioned literal examples, and a class-property co-occurrence matrix. On the CK25 Text2SPARQL challenge, QRAKEN achieves strict F1 of 0.643 ± 0.026 with GPT-4.1 mini and 0.652 ± 0.012 with GPT-5.4, representing relative gains of 30% and 32% over the strongest recomputed participant. The training-free, ontology-agnostic design and strong empirical results on CK25 suggest a practical path toward more reliable natural language interfaces for Semantic Web data, potentially benefiting knowledge graph practitioners and LLM grounding research. Ablations identify TTQL patterns as the dominant driver (+0.31 strict F1 over a shape-only baseline), while the refinement loop acts as a cheap safety net by rejecting triple patterns unsupported by the co-occurrence matrix; TTQL yields 64% higher strict F1 than auto-derived SHACL. With two local 35B 4-bit open-weight models at zero marginal cost, the same pipeline matches the strongest recomputed participant, though monolithic TTQL injection on very open cross-domain graphs remains the main limitation.

## [ML learns inverse mapping from alloy microstructure to composition and process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08165) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08165) investigates whether the inverse step of alloy development—going from an optimized microstructure and texture back to the alloy composition and processing parameters—can be learned. Using an in-house dataset of 107 magnesium alloy extrusion conditions across 14 alloys, each with optical micrographs and an X-ray texture measurement, the authors compare three microstructure/texture descriptors: conventional grain and texture statistics, a vision embedding from a pretrained image encoder, and a graph neural network on the grain network. Under 5-fold cross-validation, conventional descriptors identify the correct alloy for 65% of held-out conditions (versus 17% for always guessing the most common alloy), while learned embeddings stay below 30%; process parameters are recoverable but noisier, with microstructure roughly halving the temperature error compared to using composition alone. This work tests whether machine learning can replace expert intuition in the reverse direction of alloy design, which is traditionally done forward by tuning structure until a target property is met. If the inverse mapping can be learned reliably, it could shorten alloy development cycles and reduce the reliance on costly trial-and-error experiments, though the current results show that learned embeddings still underperform simple conventional descriptors. Because only a few alloys were cast and only a few press settings were used, both the composition and process answers are discrete, and prediction heads that pick from these known options while respecting their order worked better than heads that predict a free value. The conventional descriptors outperformed both the pretrained vision embedding and the graph neural network on the grain network for alloy identification, suggesting that simple statistics remain a strong baseline for this small dataset.

## [LFHE: Local-First Heuristic Evolution for Decentralized Learning Topology Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08176) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Local-First Heuristic Evolution (LFHE), a representation-driven rewiring framework for decentralized learning that discovers and scores candidate peers using only ego-neighborhood and friend-of-a-friend (FoF) information. The paper shows that LFHE's structural score has an exact interpretation via graph Dirichlet energy, and reports competitive performance across four image, speech, and text benchmarks. Decentralized learning is highly sensitive to communication topology under non-IID data, and LFHE offers a middle ground between purely pairwise peer selection and globally informed topology optimization. This could enable adaptive, communication-efficient topology rewiring in distributed ML systems where global graph information is impractical to collect. The structural score's sum across clients equals twice the representation Dirichlet energy, which under standard linear consensus dynamics governs the instantaneous dissipation of representation disagreement. LFHE combines this state-dependent structural signal with early exploration and degree control, while algebraic connectivity remains an offline graph diagnostic, and under bounded sparse degree its FoF candidate state stays local rather than expanding toward population-wide peer tracking.

## [Confidence-Ordering Reversal Found in Neural Decoding with Contextual Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08229) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08229) identifies a confidence-ordering reversal in neural speech decoding: when a contextual prior is applied via additive shallow fusion, errors that start at lower ranks can become more confident without any accuracy improvement. Experiments on the MEG-MASC and MOUS datasets show that the AUROC separating repairs from residual errors drops from 0.70 at initial ranks 2-3 to 0.39 at ranks 21-50, and errors starting beyond rank 20 make up 46.6% of all post-fusion errors. This finding matters because confidence scores are widely used to decide when a neural decoding system should trust its output, so a reversal means confidence can become misleading precisely for the hardest errors. It has direct implications for the reliability and safety of brain-to-language decoding systems and for selective decoding, where the authors show that reading local and prior scores separately lets the decoder answer on 74.5% of windows instead of 56.7% while keeping 92% of output sets containing the correct candidate. The paper proposes a score-level account: a repair must first close the correct candidate's initial deficit, which limits its final margin, whereas a residual error can build a large margin between two incorrect candidates. A causal intervention that changes only the fusion weight moves the reversal to deeper ranks as predicted, and under a word-level language model prior the reversal keeps moving after accuracy gain peaks, so a weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence.

Contextual priors from language models are commonly combined with local decoding scores through additive shallow fusion to improve accuracy, and confidence is typically read from the fused top-two margin. ## [zkLLMPoT Certifies LLM Training via Forward Evaluation, Not Trajectory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08258) ⭐️ 7.0/10

zkLLMPoT introduces a two-phase zero-knowledge framework that certifies auditor-defined properties of a trained LLM checkpoint through forward evaluation rather than verifying the full optimization trajectory. The trainer first commits the architecture and weights, then the auditor selects challenge sequences, and the trainer proves the objective value attained on those sequences without revealing weights or private training data. This makes certification cost independent of the number of training iterations, addressing a major barrier to auditing large models whose weights and data are private. It could enable regulators, auditors, and model buyers to verify claimed training outcomes without access to proprietary assets. The framework builds on sumcheck- and lookup-based arguments to certify Transformer computations, supporting next-token loss and task-specific audit objectives. Operator-level benchmarks show proving times of 41-59 seconds for 1.1-1.5B-parameter models and 131 seconds at 13B, with verification under half a second at sequence length 512.

**Background**: Zero-knowledge proofs let one party prove a statement is true without revealing the underlying data, and zkML applies this to machine learning computations. This shifts the audit target from the optimization trajectory to the committed model's behavior on auditor-chosen inputs.

## [Standardization Trap Exposed in Tabular Foundation Model Label Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08314) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08314) identifies a 'standardization trap' that causes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) to appear nonlinear when tested with ordinary derivatives, even if their predictions agree with a fixed-weight map. The authors propose two certificates based only on predictions at standardized labels, and across five public TFMs these certificates reject both fixed-weight prediction and sums of independent nonlinear label transformations, revealing 'joint processing' where changing one context label alters how other labels influence the prediction. The certificates depend only on predictions at standardized labels, avoiding the trap where ordinary derivatives reflect behavior outside the set of standardized labels. The authors further find that joint processing emerges with training and that attention scores carry most of the measured interaction, suggesting that TFM explanations must account for how context labels change the influence of individual examples.

Researchers propose AssemState, a zero-shot framework that decomposes diagrammatic furniture manuals into an assembly tree using anchor-guided boundary assembly states, then applies iterative after-state feedback to guide successive SE(3) pose updates validated by simulation-based release tests. Compared with the strongest prior baseline, it improves assembly-tree recovery F1 from 38.58% to 62.80% and Tree Exact Match from 28.24% to 53.92%, while on 243 part-level operations iterative refinement raises judge-accepted operations from 0 to 5.3% and reduces mean Chamfer distance from 5.4111 to 1.7744. The framework uses anchor-guided boundary assembly states to split manual pages into single-part operations, then relies on iterative after-state feedback refinement to correct SE(3) updates, with simulation-based release tests checking physical plausibility. The authors note that visually plausible candidate poses can still suffer from collision, floating, mirror-orientation errors, incomplete seating, and wrong-side attachment, and the abstract is truncated.

The paper introduces cylindrical geodesic flow matching, a geometry-aware method for paired translation of quasiperiodic cardiovascular waveforms that explicitly models phase wrapping and strictly positive amplitude. On zero-shot photoplethysmography and limited-support seismocardiography adaptation benchmarks, it reduces Hilbert Transform, L2, and Dynamic Time Warping distance by up to about 15% over the strongest competing baseline. This work shows that the geometry of the interpolation path is a critical inductive bias for flow matching on oscillatory signals, potentially improving wearable cardiovascular monitoring by enabling accurate cross-location signal translation. It could benefit researchers and engineers working on physiological signal processing and generative models for wearables. The method replaces the standard affine path in flow matching with a closed-form geodesic on the phase-amplitude cylinder, which eliminates distortions in intermediate amplitude and instantaneous frequency and converts each training pair into dense, geometry-consistent velocity supervision. The abstract is truncated and no community discussion is provided, so engagement and full experimental details remain unclear.

## [AnyBottle builds compact task-specific concept bottleneck models without annotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08552) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose AnyBottle, a method that builds compact, task-specific concept bottleneck models (CBMs) by selecting concepts from an unsupervised pool (such as a sparse autoencoder) guided by a black-box teacher trained on the same frozen backbone. Trained with nested dropout over the selection order, the resulting bottleneck predicts accurately from any concept prefix, and across six vision and two text datasets it yields fewer concepts and higher concept consistency than annotation-free baselines. This addresses a key limitation of annotation-free CBMs, which typically rely on large, static concept vocabularies that are hard to inspect and larger than any task needs. By showing that a small, discovered vocabulary can be as expressive as a much larger fixed one, AnyBottle could make interpretable machine learning more practical and scalable across domains. Each selection round adds the concept that best explains the bottleneck's current failures, with candidates restricted to regions of teacher/student disagreement, and nested dropout lets inference spend fewer concepts on confident inputs and more on hard ones. Since no stage is modality-specific, adapting to a new domain or task requires swapping only the backbone and concept pool.

Sparse autoencoders are unsupervised neural networks that learn interpretable features from unlabeled data, and nested dropout is a regularization technique that imposes a strict order on hidden units so that any prefix of the representation remains usable.

## [MINDSET: Energy-Based Schema Evolution for Long Conversational Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08586) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MINDSET introduces an energy-based memory controller that stores conversations as immutable episodes and organizes them into versioned schemas through minimum-energy state transitions, where each incoming episode can reinforce, supersede, split, or create a schema. Evaluated against 5 memory systems on 850 questions (700 LoCoMo + 150 MemoryAgentBench), it achieves the highest observed LoCoMo answer F1 and significantly improves retrieval ranking (Recall@8, MRR, nDCG@8) over the second-best method LightMem (p<0.01 after Holm correction). Long conversational agents must handle instructions and context that change over time, and MINDSET reframes long-term memory as constrained state management rather than continual summarization, potentially reducing repeated LLM calls to rewrite prior interactions. This could benefit researchers and practitioners building assistants that need to distinguish stale information from active knowledge while preserving historical states. The transition decision balances representation distortion, contradiction, historical damage, fragmentation, and internal inconsistency, while hysteresis prevents isolated contradictions from prematurely rewriting stable memory. Ablations identify controlled fragmentation and schema-aware assignment as the largest contributors to answer quality, and a 700-question cross-model evaluation with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B supported model independence.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Energy-based models (EBMs) learn an energy function over data, where low-energy states correspond to likely or stable configurations, drawing on concepts from statistical physics. Schema evolution, in databases, is the process of adapting a schema's structure over time while preserving existing data and query functionality. MINDSET applies these ideas to conversational memory, treating schema changes as minimum-energy transitions between stable memory states.

## [PPWM: Parallel Predictive World Models for Long-Horizon Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Parallel Predictive World Models (PPWM), which predict a finite-horizon trajectory in parallel while retaining causal interaction among future representations, rather than relying on state-by-state autoregressive rollouts. Across four visual-control tasks, PPWM achieved the lowest long-horizon prediction error and the highest Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) simulator success, with over a 3x average CEM planning speedup over the autoregressive LeWM baseline. This work challenges the assumption that accurate long-horizon world-model planning requires sequential autoregression, showing that parallel causal trajectory prediction can be both more accurate and more efficient. If it generalizes, it could reshape model-based reinforcement learning and planning research by removing the sequential bottleneck and reducing error accumulation in long-horizon rollouts. PPWM conditions each horizon on its causal action prefix and lets future representations interact before decoding, separating temporal causality from state-by-state output recursion. The paper formalizes autoregressive rollout as a causal trajectory map and identifies the decoded-state feedback pathway that PPWM removes, which is the key source of recursive error exposure.

## [SquidAgent Cuts Hidden Costs of Parallel LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08647) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08647) introduces SquidAgent, a cost-aware scheduler that decides layer by layer whether to parallelize a multi-agent LLM workflow. It identifies two hidden costs—re-exploration and alignment—that make parallel systems slower than serial baselines, and measures cost in predicted output tokens rather than wall-clock time because LLMs estimate tokens more reliably. Empirically, SquidAgent reports a 2.2× mean throughput improvement and a 2.6× mean wall-time speedup over Claude Code, plus a 2.0× throughput gain over the strongest multi-agent baseline. Parallelizing LLM agents is widely assumed to yield near-linear speedups, but this paper shows that assumption often fails due to coordination overhead, offering a principled criterion for when parallelism actually pays off. This matters for both researchers designing multi-agent architectures and practitioners running agentic coding or workflow tools, where unnecessary parallelism wastes tokens, latency, and money. The decision criterion states a layer should be parallelized only when its critical-path cost plus re-exploration and alignment overheads is lower than the serial cost. SquidAgent estimates all token budgets in a single planning step, forks each worker directly from the orchestrator's session to eliminate re-exploration, and replaces post-hoc reconciliation with a pre-generated shared convention block that bounds alignment cost upfront; a deterministic scheduler then applies the criterion layer by layer. As a preprint, it has not yet undergone peer review.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: LLM-based agents break complex tasks into multiple steps, and running those steps sequentially can be slow, so many systems fan work out to multiple agents in parallel. However, parallel workers do not automatically inherit the shared context that a single serial agent would have, so they may redundantly re-derive prior decisions (re-exploration) or produce inconsistent outputs that must be reconciled (alignment). SquidAgent is a scheduler that treats these overheads as first-class costs and only parallelizes layers where the math favors it.

## [RL Framework Learns When to Refine Neural-Operator PDE Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06883) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a budgeted adaptive neural-operator solving framework in which a global Fourier neural operator advances the full field, a local operator proposes patch-wise residual corrections, and a macro policy decides when and how much of a finite refinement budget to spend. It also proposes rollout-verified policy improvement (RV-PI), which evaluates refinement counts through actual continuation rollouts and accepts updates only when held-out trajectory error improves, achieving a three-seed mean trajectory relative L2 error of 0.6910 on shallow-water and 0.09954 on the forcing-driven Brusselator benchmark. This work addresses a real bottleneck in scientific machine learning: autoregressive neural-operator surrogates accumulate spatially and temporally varying errors, and naive refinement wastes limited compute. By showing that the value of a local correction depends on its downstream effect on the trajectory rather than only its immediate error reduction, the method could enable more accurate long-horizon PDE simulation under fixed computational budgets, benefiting researchers in neural operators, reinforcement learning, and scientific computing. RV-PI converts long-horizon advantages into conservative policy targets and accepts an update only when held-out trajectory error improves, which adds rollout-based verification cost but guards against harmful policy changes. On shallow-water with a 32-intervention budget it improves over immediate-only policy improvement by 5.37% and RandomMacro by 2.41%, while on Brusselator with a 76-intervention budget it improves by 2.31% and 5.32% respectively.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Neural operators are a class of models that learn mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces, allowing them to serve as fast surrogates for families of partial differential equations (PDEs) without retraining for each new parameter or condition. The Fourier neural operator (FNO) is a widely used variant whose integral kernel is parameterized in Fourier space, making it efficient for problems with periodic or smooth structures. When such surrogates are deployed autoregressively over long horizons, prediction errors vary across space and time, creating a refinement-allocation problem in which only a limited number of local corrections can be applied along a trajectory.

## [Low-Rank Equilibrium Computation for APT vs. Moving Target Defense Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06885) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.06885v2) introduces DLR-NE, a Dynamical Low-Rank Nash Equilibrium algorithm for computing equilibria in zero-sum stochastic games between advanced persistent threats (APTs) and moving target defense (MTD) in industrial control systems. The authors prove that attack and defense influence matrices are intrinsically low-rank, yielding a certified low-rank approximation with explicit error bounds, geometric convergence, and an O(nr^2) per-step cost that is a Theta(n/r^2) speedup over full-rank value iteration. Equilibrium computation for game-theoretic security models has been prohibitively expensive at industrial scale and lacked certified robustness, so this work could make MTD deployment practical for real ICS environments. It bridges game theory, security, and numerical linear algebra, offering both scalability and provable sensitivity bounds that matter to defenders and control-system operators. The method augments the rank-r search space each iteration, regularizes the core matrix spectrum, and retracts via truncated SVD; Theorem 2 shows geometric convergence to a neighborhood whose error decomposes into five interpretable sources, and Corollary 1 shows a single weight trades accuracy against a certified sensitivity bound under core-matrix perturbations. Six experiments on a nonlinear power-system testbed report 94% parameter compression at 2.3% utility loss, with code and data publicly available.

Dynamical low-rank approximation is a differential-equation-based technique for efficiently approximating large time-dependent matrices, and this paper applies that idea to the Bellman operator of the security game.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.06892) analyzes the cost of enforcing the Pareto optimality (PO) and population monotonicity (PMC) axioms in linear reward models for language model alignment. By relaxing the linear model to allow per-candidate slack, the authors show the optimal total slack needed to satisfy the axioms with margin η is bounded by O(1) when η is at most O(1/m²) for m candidates, and prove this rate is tight up to constants. This work addresses a fundamental theoretical limitation in reward modeling for AI alignment: prior results show that standard linear reward fitting (including BTL) necessarily violates key social choice axioms. The finding that a bounded relaxation suffices suggests practical alignment methods can be designed to respect these axioms without abandoning linear rewards, which are the only rewards evaluable on unseen responses. The paper introduces a new method that charges the linear part for each comparison it gets wrong, simultaneously minimizing total slack and the number of violations via a trade-off parameter λ. It proves the total slack is monotone but saturating in λ, staying below (η + Δ√d)⌊m²/4⌋, where Δ and d are the diameter and dimension of the feature representation; experiments on synthetic and real preference data show the method outperforms linear BTL.

## [AttSVD: Prompt-Adaptive Low-Rank KV Cache Compression via Attention-Guided SVD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06927) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AttSVD introduces a training-free KV cache compression method that keeps every token but stores it more cheaply along the feature axis, using an online per-prompt truncated SVD whose basis is derived from each prompt's own attention geometry. It offers two decode-time caching strategies (accumulating and streaming) plus two adaptive refinements, and across multiple models on an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite it matches the dense cache while using up to 50% of the KV-cache memory. Long-context inference is bottlenecked by the KV cache, which grows linearly with context length and dominates memory; most training-free fixes irreversibly evict tokens along the sequence axis, whereas AttSVD compresses along the feature axis without discarding any token. This could make long-context and agentic deployments substantially cheaper without retraining, and the same factors yield free per-head interpretability about effective rank and the geometry attention consumes. The method is training-free and prompt-adaptive: a per-matrix energy rule independently sizes the logit space and the attention mass, and an attention-aware basis truncation operates only in the subspaces attention actually reads, preserving both attention logits and attention output. Persistent per-head KV memory is cut in proportion to the retained rank, though the abstract reports no experimental tables and the work remains a preprint without community discussion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: In autoregressive transformers, the key-value (KV) cache stores the keys and values of all previous tokens so that generation does not recompute them, but its size grows linearly with context length — for example, handling 1M tokens with Llama 3.1-70B in float16 can require up to 330GB of memory. Low-rank approximation via singular value decomposition (SVD) replaces a matrix with a lower-rank one by keeping only its most important singular directions, which is the mathematical tool AttSVD applies to the KV cache. Prior training-free KV compression mostly evicts low-importance tokens along the sequence axis, an irreversible choice that AttSVD avoids by compressing along the feature axis instead.

## [CrystalJev reframes atomistic foundation models as fast decision-makers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06985) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CrystalJev treats a frozen interatomic potential as a fast probabilistic decision-maker, querying it once per unrelaxed structure and returning typed answers with calibrated probabilities and finite-sample guarantees. Across 65 Matbench Discovery models, a single forward pass decides nearly as well as a full relaxation at roughly one-thirtieth of the cost, and a value-of-information rule routes slower computation only where decisions can change. This could substantially cut the compute cost of high-throughput materials screening, since most hypothetical crystals can be triaged with a single cheap forward pass instead of a full relaxation. It also gives the AI-for-science community a principled uncertainty-quantification layer that turns thresholded energy predictions into calibrated probabilities, which matters for deciding which candidates deserve expensive DFT verification. The method is validated in a registered prospective test with 700 new density-functional calculations, where single-pass forecasts calibrated only on existing data over-stated the stable fraction of unseen candidates (5.8%) by at most 2.1 percentage points. The same decision layer is reported to answer electronic, mechanical and molecular questions, not just stability.

## [TARE Exposes Flawed Backdoor-Defense Cost Measurements in BackdoorBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06994) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.06994) shows that three of BackdoorBench's sixteen attacks—WaNet, BPP, and Input-Aware—ship a MultiStepLR scheduler that never fires, leaving their victim models under-trained and the least accurate in 30 of 31 public CIFAR cells at ≤5%. This misconfiguration causes fine-tuning-family defenses to report negative removal costs, and the authors propose TARE, a method that measures defense cost on a never-poisoned twin model trained with the same recipe, schedule, and seed. This finding undermines the reliability of backdoor-defense leaderboards: 2 of 48 citing defense papers base a no-cost claim on these flawed cells, and re-running TSBD and CGD shows they also 'gain' on a never-poisoned model. It highlights a serious reproducibility concern that could mislead the security and ML research communities about which defenses actually work. A 2×2 editing of only the scheduler line isolates the cause: the sign of the fine-tuning family's clean-model cost reverses both ways while its published gain on the annealed victim only shrinks toward zero, with 44/44 seeds following the schedule, replicated on BPP, FT-SAM, CIFAR-100, and VGG19-BN, and induced in a second toolkit. On the BadNets grid, seven of eight defenses charge the never-poisoned twin (+0.13 for fine-tuning to +5.70 points for I-BAU), while ABL destroys it; the authors ship a three-key patch, a signed tare column (7 attacks × 8 defenses), and TARE-Z, a twin-free estimator for seed-stable defenses.

**Background**: BackdoorBench is a widely used benchmark and leaderboard for evaluating backdoor attacks and defenses on deep learning models, providing implementations and thousands of evaluation pairs. Backdoor attacks implant hidden triggers during training so a model misbehaves on specific inputs, while defenses aim to remove this behavior; the 'removal cost' is typically measured as the drop in clean accuracy after applying a defense. MultiStepLR is a PyTorch learning-rate scheduler that decays the learning rate at predefined milestones, and if it never fires, the model never anneals and remains under-trained.

## [MaskAhead: Training-Free KV Cache Eviction for Block Diffusion LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06996) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces MaskAhead, a training-free method that uses a single mask-query-based ranking mechanism to handle both KV cache selection and eviction in block diffusion language models. A quantized variant, Q-MaskAhead, computes selection and attention directly from low-bit KV, and on long-prompt QA MaskAhead cuts KV memory by 9.5x on average with only a 1.2-point mean F1 loss, while Q-MaskAhead reaches 20.1x reduction with a 2.3-point loss. Block diffusion language models keep a large KV cache throughout generation and attend to it at every denoising step, which limits both memory capacity and generation speed. MaskAhead shows that this bottleneck can be substantially reduced without any retraining, making long-context and long-generation inference more practical for researchers and deployers of diffusion-based LLMs. Current-block masks guide selection while probes of upcoming masked blocks guide eviction, with both ranking KV entries by their estimated contribution to the attention output. Experiments on Fast-dLLM-v2, DreamReasoner, and LLaDA2.0-mini cover long-generation reasoning, long-prompt QA, and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, and in a batch-32 systems profile MaskAhead achieves 1.23x end-to-end and 1.68x decode-stage speedups over dense inference.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: KV cache stores the key and value tensors of previously processed tokens so a model can reuse them instead of recomputing attention from scratch, but it grows with sequence length and becomes a memory and latency bottleneck. Block diffusion language models, such as BD3-LMs, interpolate between autoregressive and discrete diffusion generation by denoising tokens block by block, and they must attend to the full KV cache at every denoising step. KV cache eviction methods aim to discard less important entries to save memory, and MaskAhead adapts this idea to the block diffusion setting by using the model's own attention masks as a ranking signal.

## [TRIAGE Stabilizes Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07043) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper introduces TRIAGE, a direction-aware stabilization method that mitigates mismatch-induced instability in native NVFP4 reinforcement learning. It distinguishes locally amplifying from contracting policy-gradient updates and selectively rebalances them, achieving full-precision-level performance on five math reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B while providing up to 2.3x higher rollout throughput than BF16. Low-precision execution can substantially accelerate RL for large language models, but discrepancies between learner and sampler execution can destabilize policy optimization. TRIAGE shows that native NVFP4 W4A4 training can be made stable without sacrificing accuracy, potentially making large-scale RL post-training much more efficient on NVIDIA Blackwell hardware. TRIAGE uses segment-level diagnosis to selectively rebalance policy-gradient updates and applies bounded repair to residual severe mismatch, modifying the optimization objective while retaining native NVFP4 4-bit weight-and-activation (W4A4) forward execution on both sampler and learner. The authors observe an early imbalance favoring negative-advantage, negative-gap updates whose tail tokens concentrate in a small fraction of response segments before mismatch spreads globally.

## [Muon Optimizer's Theory Breaks on Convolutions, Yet Still Works](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07103) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07103) formalizes Muon's optimization objective directly in convolutional operator geometry and introduces Convolutional Newton-Schulz (Conv-NS), which approximates the polar factor while preserving kernel support. Experiments show Conv-NS and standard reshape-based Muon achieve comparable accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, despite the theoretical mismatch. This work exposes a gap between Muon's theoretical foundations and its practical implementation on convolutional layers, which are central to most vision models. It suggests that exact convolutional orthogonalization may overconstrain updates, opening new directions for optimizer design and raising questions about how much theory is needed for empirical success. Conv-NS approximates the polar factor in convolutional operator geometry using Newton-Schulz iterations while preserving kernel support, unlike reshape-based Muon which flattens 4D tensors into matrices. Both methods are computationally efficient, but the theoretically aligned Conv-NS does not outperform the reshape shortcut, suggesting exact convolutional orthogonalization may be too restrictive.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Muon is an optimizer for hidden 2D weight matrices that applies Newton-Schulz iterations to orthogonalize the momentum matrix before updating weights, and it has set training speed records for NanoGPT and CIFAR-10. Convolutional kernels, however, are stored as 4D tensors, so standard implementations reshape them into 2D matrices—a shortcut that breaks Muon's theoretical interpretation. Newton-Schulz iteration is a matrix polynomial method for computing polar factors, and polar decomposition factors a matrix into a partial isometry and a positive semidefinite matrix.

## [Linear Probes on Residual Streams Predict LLM Judge Position Flips](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07115) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07115) shows that regularized linear probes trained on residual stream activations recorded immediately before an LLM judge's initial verdict can predict when that judge will flip its decision due to candidate order. Evaluated on 534 JudgeBench pairs across three Qwen3 judges and Llama-3.1-8B, the probes reach AUROCs of .621-.850 and beat a combined baseline of verbalized confidence, verdict-label logits, response lengths, and the initial choice by .062-.113 AUROC. Position bias is a well-known reliability problem for LLM-as-a-judge pipelines, and detecting a flip normally requires judging each pair twice, doubling evaluation cost. If pre-verdict activations can flag susceptibility to order, practitioners could avoid redundant judgments or correct biased verdicts, making LLM evaluation cheaper and more trustworthy. The probes were validated with nested grouped cross-validation, and when trained on JudgeBench and then frozen they achieved AUROCs of .685-.853 on 1,802 MT-Bench comparisons without any MT-Bench fitting or recalibration. The results indicate that pre-verdict residual stream activations carry information about order susceptibility that goes beyond non-activation predictors such as confidence and logits.

**Background**: The residual stream is the cumulative hidden-state representation that flows through a transformer's layers, formed by adding each sublayer's output to the running state; it is a common target for interpretability research. Linear probing trains a simple linear classifier on such internal activations to test whether a concept is linearly encoded. JudgeBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based judges on challenging response pairs in knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding, while MT-Bench is a widely used multi-turn benchmark for comparing model responses.

## [PEV Attack Jailbreaks Six Open-Weight LLMs via Random Embedding Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07125) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper introduces Perturbed Embedding Vector (PEV), a jailbreaking attack that adds independent Gaussian noise to a prompt's embedding representations to bypass safety mechanisms in six open-weight LLMs of various sizes. PEV achieves unsafe responses across all models for all prompts in the JailbreakBench benchmark, with the first successful jailbreak typically arriving within one minute per prompt. This attack is significantly cheaper than prior jailbreaking methods that require gradient computations, per-prompt optimization, or weight modification, lowering the barrier for adversarial exploitation of open-weight models. It highlights a persistent safety gap in widely adopted open-weight LLMs and is likely to spur new research into embedding-level defenses and alignment robustness. PEV simply samples additive Gaussian noise in the embedding space with no further manipulation, and the average compute cost to obtain the first successful attack is up to an order of magnitude lower than previous attacks. The authors note that while perturbations pose a major security risk, understanding LLM behavior under embedding perturbations is also a valuable tool for exploring model dynamics.

**Background**: Open-weight LLMs are models whose trained parameters (weights and biases) are publicly released, allowing anyone to download, run, and often fine-tune them; they are contrasted with proprietary models whose weights remain closed. Embeddings are numerical vector representations that capture the semantic meaning of input tokens and serve as the first internal representation an LLM processes. Jailbreaking refers to crafting inputs that cause a model to bypass its safety training and produce harmful or policy-violating content, and JailbreakBench is an open robustness benchmark that defines 100 harmful behaviors alongside 100 matched benign ones to systematically track attack and defense progress.

## [CroissantMiner Benchmarks Automated Croissant Metadata Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07132) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released CroissantMiner, the first benchmark for end-to-end evaluation of Croissant metadata extraction from ML dataset papers, comprising 602 papers (102 with human-validated gold annotations and 500 with LLM-generated silver annotations) covering core and Responsible AI fields. Evaluating frontier models, open-weight models, and four agentic architectures, they found single-pass full-context extraction consistently outperforms decomposed agentic approaches, with the largest gap on long-form RAI fields. Populating Croissant metadata is labor-intensive and requires careful reading of dataset documentation, so automating it could substantially reduce the burden of making ML datasets machine-readable and improve reproducibility and responsible AI practices. The finding that single-pass extraction beats agentic architectures also challenges the assumption that more complex pipelines are always better for structured information extraction. The benchmark uses a two-tier evaluation framework combining rule-based scoring with an LLM judge selected via human audit, and the authors note that current systems remain far from reliable on long-form RAI fields that require synthesizing information scattered across a paper rather than copying it from one location. The benchmark, evaluation code, judge audit, live demo, and an open leaderboard are all released.

## [SPEAR: Five Principles for Interactive Human-Agent Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07204) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new position paper (arXiv:2610.07204) by Tao Long and one co-author proposes SPEAR, a framework of five pillars for interactive human-agent alignment: Specification, Process, Evaluation, Adaptation, and Recalibration. It argues that alignment should be reframed from a one-time pre-deployment optimization into an ongoing interaction design problem in situated, long-term, and social contexts. This reframing matters because current alignment pipelines—collecting human feedback, learning preferences, fine-tuning, and deploying—under-specify what happens once AI agents act on users' behalf over time. By connecting alignment to HCI and interaction design, SPEAR could influence how researchers and designers build, evaluate, and maintain agentic systems that must earn and keep user trust. The five pillars map to concrete questions: how people express intent and build shared understanding (Specification), how agents decide when to act, ask, defer, or pause (Process), how people judge success (Evaluation), how agents adapt across repeated use (Adaptation), and how people adjust trust, expectations, and behavior (Recalibration). As a position paper, it offers a conceptual bridge to HCI foundations rather than empirical validation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: AI alignment generally refers to steering AI systems toward a person's or group's intended goals, preferences, or ethical principles, and a system is considered aligned if it advances those intended objectives. Most recent alignment work treats this as a pre-deployment optimization problem: gather human feedback, learn preferences or principles, fine-tune the model, and deploy. SPEAR builds on older HCI and interaction design traditions to argue that alignment must also be maintained and repaired continuously after deployment.

## [DRMoET: Distributionally Robust Training Improves MoE Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07207) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Distributionally Robust MoE Training (DRMoET), a drop-in objective that treats layer-wise experts as endogenous robustness groups and optimizes high-loss routing outcomes instead of merely equalizing traffic. At 10.3B total parameters and 67B training tokens, DRMoET improves the seven-task average from 0.6625 to 0.6767, outperforming both standard FLAME-MoE and auxiliary-loss-free balancing (0.6431). This work reframes routing robustness—not just load balance—as a practical objective for reliable sparse MoE scaling, potentially influencing how large MoE models are trained. It matters for practitioners building MoE transformers who care about reliability under imperfect routing, and it offers a drop-in objective that preserves standard MoE computation. DRMoET updates a per-layer expert distribution via an entropy-regularized softmax rule on EMA-smoothed, activation-weighted expert losses, strengthening plausible non-top routing paths. Mechanistic analyses show lower expert-loss variance with nearly unchanged mean loss, 4.3% lower excess loss under forced mid-k misrouting, and improved domain-expert specialization; the project page and code are at https://drmoet.github.io/.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformers scale model capacity by activating only a few experts per token, but this sparsity creates a hidden reliability problem: when routing is imperfect, load-balanced models may send tokens to experts that are insufficiently trained for the assigned inputs. Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) is a framework that optimizes model performance against the worst-case distribution within an uncertainty set, and DRMoET adapts this idea to MoE routing. FLAME-MoE is a training recipe used here as the baseline, with Adam optimizer, maximum learning rate 3e-4, global batch size 1024, sequence length 2048, and a Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule.

Researchers released TIDE 2.0, an MIT-licensed, model-agnostic engine for de-identifying clinical notes, along with TIDE2-Sentry, a recognizer distilled from a large language model. The system uses cryptographic surrogates with no stored linkage table and per-patient, interval-preserving date shifts, achieving span-level recall of 0.88 in-domain and 0.77 on a second institution's corpus at precision 0.88 and 0.87. Clinical notes are essential for research but cannot be shared until protected health information is removed, and existing approaches like redaction or date blanking destroy clinical content and temporal structure. The engine separates an interchangeable recognizer from a keyed anonymizer, generates surrogates cryptographically without a stored linkage table, assigns the same surrogate to each value across all occurrences under a given key, and ensures releases under a new key cannot be linked to earlier ones. The recognizer is available under a gated research-use agreement rather than a fully open license.

## [MWRL Uses Single Verifier Bit to Learn Minimal Witness Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07226) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL), which formalizes the problem of identifying multiple minimal sufficient witnesses and solves it using only a single black-box verifier bit. MWRL credits each sampled proposal by the marginal coverage its removal would cost the group union, and the authors derive both a value iteration planner that recovers the full witness family and a policy gradient method that scales to large language models. Most reinforcement learning methods are designed to find a single optimal solution, so they tend to return one witness or redundant supersets when a problem has multiple valid explanations. By making entire witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL could improve explainable AI, scientific discovery, and any domain where understanding all irreducible causes of an outcome matters. The credit assignment is derived directly from the problem definition and unifies minimality with the recovery of alternative witnesses, while the method assumes a monotonic certified region where a rollout ends in a proposed subset that the verifier accepts or rejects. Experiments show MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, whereas baselines return redundant supersets or a single witness, and code is available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: A minimal sufficient witness is the smallest set of conditions that is enough to produce a given outcome — essentially what we mean by an explanation, mechanism, or reason. In statistics, a sufficient statistic captures all information a dataset provides about a parameter, and minimal witnesses play an analogous role in computation and science. Reinforcement learning typically optimizes toward one solution, so extending it to recover multiple minimal explanations from only a binary verifier signal is a nontrivial credit-assignment challenge.

## [AMU: Lineage-Aware Memory Governance for Enterprise AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07258) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the Analytical Memory Unit (AMU), a memory schema that attaches a full derivation (lineage) graph to every cached result in a shared agent memory store, gated by a retrieval policy that serves a hit only when the requester is authorized for every column touched. The authors prove by construction that the policy blocks retrieval of results derived from sensitive columns outside a requester's permissions at O(n) worst case, and across six experiments lineage-gated retrieval eliminates the 18.8–25.5% cross-department leakage suffered by naive content-gated memory while retaining 81.5–82.6% of memory reuse at 13.8 microsecond worst-case overhead. Existing agent-memory systems such as MemGPT, Zep, and A-MEM gate retrieval by content, ownership, and role rather than derivation, so they can miss a cached insight that embeds a forbidden column. This work addresses a real governance gap for enterprise AI agents sharing memory across departments, and its lineage-gated design could influence future agent memory architectures while supporting EU AI Act compliance. The guarantee is conditional: it holds only if lineage recording is complete, and eliminating measured leakage required 75–90% recorded lineage completeness, so the authors treat 90% as a conservative deployment target. The proof excludes derived features that encode sensitive information without naming their source, and a real-agent proof-of-concept with LLM-generated SQL showed zero leaks over 9 round-trips and caught two conflicts automatically, though the authors stress this is a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of production viability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Enterprise AI agents increasingly share a common memory store so that insights computed by one department or session can be reused by others, improving efficiency but creating new privacy risks. Prior memory systems like MemGPT (which manages tiered, self-editing memory), Zep (a temporal knowledge graph memory layer), and A-MEM (an agentic memory system inspired by Zettelkasten) control what an agent can retrieve based on content, ownership, or role. Data lineage—tracking how a result was derived from source columns—is a well-established concept in data governance, and this paper applies it to agent memory so that access control follows the derivation path rather than just the stored content.

## [Scale-Invariant Training Fixes Scale Bias in Time Series Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07324) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07324) shows that affine scaling methods like Reversible Instance Normalization (RevIN) cause "scale-contaminated training" (ScaleCon), where each series' gradient is multiplied by b^p, making high-scale series dominate. The authors prove that computing loss on scaled targets yields scale-invariant training (ScaleIn) for any scale-equivariant scaler and degree-p homogeneous residual loss, and show it lowers MASE in all 24 architecture-benchmark comparisons, with average reductions of 18.8% on GIFT-Eval and 21.9% on M-competitions. This identifies a fundamental, previously overlooked flaw in how time series foundation models are pretrained, affecting nearly all existing pipelines that use RevIN-style normalization. Because the fix is a one-line code change and consistently improves accuracy across architectures and benchmarks, it could become a standard convention in the rapidly growing TSFM field. The theoretical result holds for any scale-equivariant scaler and residual loss homogeneous of degree p, including MSE, MAE, and Quantile Loss; the paper notes that existing TSFMs use both objectives with no consistent reporting convention. Gains also extend to supervised neural forecasting, lowering MASE in 16 of 20 matched settings, and most pipelines can adopt ScaleIn with a one-line code change.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on large, heterogeneous collections of time series whose value magnitudes can differ by orders of magnitude. Reversible Instance Normalization (RevIN) is a widely used technique that normalizes each input window by its own mean and standard deviation, then reverses the transform before computing the loss. The paper shows this reversal re-weights gradients by the series' scale, so large-magnitude series disproportionately influence training.

## [RelayMoE: Ring-Based Routing Cuts Distributed MoE Training Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07333) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.07333) introduces RelayMoE, a ring-based execution model for distributed Mixture-of-Experts training that avoids constructing the full top-k-expanded dispatch buffer used by standard all-to-all dispatchers. Evaluated on 30B–57B production MoE models, RelayMoE achieves a 2× average speedup over Megatron-LM in single-layer experiments and up to 2.02× higher throughput in full-model training under the same GPU memory budget. As MoE models scale to hundreds of experts and higher top-k routing, peak memory is dominated by the MoE block rather than attention, making dispatch buffers a critical bottleneck. RelayMoE's memory savings could enable longer sequences, larger batches, or less attention recomputation, potentially influencing future large-scale MoE system designs. RelayMoE selects between expert routing and token routing based on communication volume and overlaps transfers with computation, while its ring structure supports memory-efficient recomputation during backward by reconstructing expert intermediates per hop and releasing them before the next hop. In full-model training it extends the largest tested trainable sequence length by up to 2.85×.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a small number of experts via top-k gating, so a single token can be replicated across k experts, expanding intermediate buffers. In distributed training, expert parallelism uses all-to-all communication to dispatch tokens to the GPUs holding the relevant experts, and the standard dispatcher must materialize the entire top-k-expanded buffer at once. Ring-based execution, common in distributed training topologies, circulates data around a ring of devices so that computation can proceed on local chunks instead of requiring a global buffer.
