The paper formalizes when a summary is sufficient for intervention decisions and quantifies the utility lost when it is not, showing that strictly increasing recalibration preserves the threshold policy class and cannot recover the missing distinction. ## [Refusal-Gated Decoding Preserves LLM Refusals at High Temperatures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20791) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2607.20791v2) proposes refusal-gated decoding (RGD), a sequential decoding method that preserves a model's greedy refusal response at high temperatures while sampling all other prompts from the exact high-temperature distribution. Across seven models and three benchmark datasets at T=2.0, RGD raises greedy-refusal preservation from 91.9% under direct sampling to 98.3% on average, adding only 2.2-4.3% to median per-request latency for non-refusals. High-temperature sampling is widely used to increase output diversity, but it is known to weaken LLM refusal behavior, creating a safety-versus-diversity tradeoff. RGD shows this tradeoff can be largely avoided without replacing the model's own refusal decision with a separate safety classifier or altering the output distribution for every prompt, which matters for anyone deploying LLMs that need both creative sampling and reliable safety refusals. RGD runs a short greedy probe that reuses the prompt's KV cache and exits as soon as it becomes incompatible with a learned set of refusal prefixes; it returns the greedy response if the probe stays compatible, otherwise it discards the probe and samples from the original prompt. Unlike prompt-screening baselines that route many greedy non-refusals to greedy decoding, RGD keeps at least 98.1% of greedy non-refusals on unchanged high-temperature sampling, and a residual-stream variant lowers the latency overhead to at most 0.5% with comparable routing accuracy.

The KV cache stores key-value vectors from previous tokens so autoregressive models avoid recomputing attention over the whole prefix at each step, which is what makes RGD's short probe cheap.

## [WebRider: Persona-Conditioned Intent Controllers for Live-Web Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06704) ⭐️ 7.0/10

WebRider introduces persona-conditioned intent controllers that formalize delegated web tasks as 'intent contracts' — operational records of goals, constraints, evidence obligations, answer form, and task-local persona controls. A full live audit found that a strong controller completes 99.2% of tasks but honors all policy constraints in only 38.8% of cases, and the team released RiderBench, a benchmark of 4,096 live-web contracts across 42 public websites. The finding that finishing a task does not imply fidelity exposes a critical blind spot in how live-web agents are currently evaluated, since a plausible final answer can conceal policy violations. This work could shift evaluation metrics and agent design toward auditing the browsing path itself, affecting researchers, developers, and users who delegate sensitive web tasks to AI assistants. WebRider uses a three-layer hierarchical architecture: a top-layer controller maintains the contract and decides whether to browse, ask, stop, block, or answer; a middle layer realizes intentions as guarded executable actions; and a tool layer executes them via browser, search, and maps tools. The guarded middle interface also serves as a training signal, and an 8B action-policy model trained through it outperforms executable-only baselines under a fixed controller.

## [RCV: A Lightweight Wrapper to Adapt and Monitor Safety Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14089) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce Regime-Conditional Verification (RCV), a lightweight wrapper that estimates, from a safety classifier's internal representations, the probability that each prediction disagrees with the deployer's policy, then selectively corrects likely-wrong predictions without retraining the classifier. Across three off-the-shelf safety classifiers and two benchmark datasets, RCV improved policy adherence in every combination, catching up to 0.81 of previously missed unsafe content, and in a ten-campaign deployment study it detected every attack campaign held out of its training. Deployed safety classifiers often encode the policy learned during training rather than the deployer's desired policy, and their accuracy degrades as traffic evolves, so a retraining-free way to realign and monitor them could make LLM safety systems more reliable and cheaper to maintain. The same correctness estimates double as a label-free distribution-shift signal, giving operators a practical maintenance loop for dynamic production environments. RCV estimates correctness from the classifier's internal representations and uses those estimates both to selectively correct predictions and to detect drift, updating only the correctness-estimation layer and resorting to classifier fine-tuning only when repair fails within a label budget. The approach was validated on three off-the-shelf classifiers and two benchmark datasets, with a deployment study of ten attack campaigns; in the maintenance census most drift episodes were repaired without updating the classifier, and fine-tuning was reserved for residual episodes.

## [Action Shaping: Policies Absorb What They Can Express](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32752) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.32752v2) introduces 'action shaping,' the action-channel counterpart to reward shaping, and states a principle: a trainable policy absorbs an action offset if its own output layer can reproduce that offset exactly, and what is absorbed can be removed at deployment with the return intact. The minimal instance is a zero-initialized linear head behind a learnable gate added to an actor-critic setup, and across 20 tasks removing the head costs almost nothing. Reward shaping has a well-known theorem guaranteeing that potential-based terms can be removed without changing the optimal policy, but the analogous practice of adding an action offset during training and dropping it at deployment has lacked any such guarantee. This work supplies the missing condition, mechanism, and diagnostic, which could change how RL practitioners handle action offsets and auxiliary action heads in policy optimization. The key condition is exact reproduction rather than capacity: a nonlinear head with more parameters is not absorbed, but in a paired control, adding one linear path to a nonlinear base head restores absorption. Exact reproduction creates a flat direction in the loss that gradient noise drifts along, and the offset's amplitude serves as a pre-removal diagnostic for what dropping the head will cost.

Test-time continual learning refers to agents acquiring, consolidating, and refining knowledge during deployment without catastrophic forgetting or repeated large-scale retraining.

## [BitNest Embeds Low-Precision Draft Inside Target Model for Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02800) ⭐️ 7.0/10

BitNest introduces a bit-nested speculative decoding framework that embeds a low-precision draft model directly into the higher-precision target model, sharing a single physical weight representation. Instead of deriving a draft from a predefined target, it first constructs a strong low-precision base and then recovers the higher-precision target through residual refinement, achieving an average speculative acceptance rate of 95.2% and 1.48–1.61x end-to-end speedup over FP16 autoregressive decoding across multiple 7B–8B edge-friendly LLMs. Speculative decoding typically requires a separate draft model or weight representation, which adds non-negligible memory overhead on resource-constrained devices. By eliminating that extra memory footprint while preserving target-model quality, BitNest could make faster LLM inference practical on edge devices and in memory-limited deployment scenarios. BitNest extends its progressive-precision design to the KV cache for long-context inference, and on LLaMA models supported by all representative self-speculative baselines it achieves consistently competitive or higher decoding speedup. The approach targets 7B–8B edge-friendly LLMs and diverse workloads, though the abstract does not detail the specific bit widths used for the low-precision base.

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by using a lightweight draft model to propose multiple tokens that a larger target model then verifies in parallel, but it usually requires an additional draft model or weight representation. ## [Feasible-Future Decoding Fixes Safety Gap in VLA Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05166) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.05166v2) identifies a "feasibility-likelihood gap" in frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies, where a locally safe action can eliminate all policy-supported routes to safe task completion. The authors derive the exact next-block marginal of the history-conditioned policy-environment trajectory law restricted to safe completion, and propose VICS-G, an alarm-triggered, training-free reranker that lowers mean cumulative safety cost by 1.9%-57.5% across six Safety-CHORES settings. This work matters because it shows that likelihood-based action selection in VLA policies is insufficient for safety, and offers a practical, retraining-free method to keep robots on viable paths to task completion. It could influence how safe robot policies are deployed in real-world manipulation and navigation, where a single locally safe but globally dead-end action can cause task failure or harm. The method derives a candidate-dependent feasible-future mass whose support indicates whether safe completion remains possible under the frozen continuation process, and whose magnitude measures preserved weighted safe-completion mass. Since exact online evaluation is impractical, the authors use a selective finite-candidate approximation with conditions for recovering the best retained viable candidate, and VICS-G stays within 2.5 percentage points of policy sampling in success and 0.82 steps in mean episode length.

## [Concord Framework Fixes Stale Context in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05281) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Concord, a context coherence framework that links each tool observation in an agent's context to its source, detects when that source changes, and applies configurable policies to update, annotate, or suppress stale observations before reuse. They also introduce ConcordBench, where previously observed file contents become stale after edits, and report that Concord matches the oracle on recover count across three frontier models while using 46.4% fewer tokens than the strongest non-oracle baseline. This addresses a correctness bug rather than a token-efficiency problem: agents that reuse outdated tool observations can make false claims about the current state of a workspace, which is especially dangerous in coding, file-editing, and multi-agent workflows where data sources are mutable. By making staleness handling a runtime-level concern, Concord could influence how agent runtimes are designed and how context management is standardized across frameworks. Concord is designed to be runtime-agnostic and resource-agnostic, so it can be extended to new runtime-resource settings, and its handling policies are configurable rather than hard-coded. The evaluation is limited to a constructed benchmark (ConcordBench) focused on file contents going stale after edits, so real-world generalization to other mutable sources remains to be tested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents often ground their reasoning in observations returned by tools, such as reading a file from a workspace, and they keep those observations in their context window as the conversation proceeds. If the underlying source is later modified by a user, another agent, or an external tool, the model still holds only the old content and may reason from it as if it were current. Existing agent runtimes offer little support for telling the model that a previously observed fact has gone stale, which leads to outdated observations being reused and incorrect claims about the workspace state.

TeleTune is a new framework that learns a textual skill library from offline user telemetry logs, without recorded goals and without replaying past activity, by using action-prediction errors to propose and validate library edits. ## [LHM-Humanoid Enables Reset-Free Long-Horizon Object Transport in Cluttered Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16943) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces LHM-Humanoid, a method that enables a physically simulated humanoid to repeatedly walk to a displaced object, lift it, carry it past obstacles, and place it at a goal within a single uninterrupted take, without any resets between cycles. It frames the transition between motion cycles as a two-sided recoverability problem and uses two goal-conditioned controllers—one for the fetch-carry-place cycle with learned release-and-retreat, and one to take over from the resulting state distribution—distilled into a single reset-free policy. This work addresses a key limitation in physics-based human motion control, where motions are typically short, isolated clips that require re-initialization, and could advance applications in humanoid robotics, animation, and simulation by enabling continuous, realistic long-horizon behaviors. It also provides a new learning-based approach to the challenging transition problem that naive end-to-end reinforcement learning fails to solve. The method is evaluated across 350 cluttered layouts spanning four room types, and it outperforms end-to-end RL, hierarchical RL, and prior physics-based human-scene-interaction methods on both seen and unseen scenes. Both controllers are regularized by an adversarial motion prior, and the key challenge is that every placement leaves the character off-balance in a non-canonical pose, requiring the terminal state to be steered into a recoverable region.

The joint-distribution Wasserstein discrepancy provably upper-bounds the conditional discrepancy, making it a practical surrogate for alignment. The method is differentiable and readily compatible with gradient-based optimization, and code is available at an anonymous repository.

A new arXiv paper (2511.00053v2) proposes a Quadratic Direct Forecast (QDF) method that replaces standard mean squared error with a quadratic-form weighted learning objective. The weighting matrix uses off-diagonal elements to capture label autocorrelation between future steps and non-uniform diagonals to assign heterogeneous task weights across different forecast horizons, with the matrix adaptively updated during training. Most existing forecasting models are trained with MSE, which treats every future step as an independent and equally weighted task, introducing bias and limiting accuracy. By correcting both the autocorrelation bias and the uniform-weighting assumption, QDF could become a drop-in training objective that improves a wide range of forecasting architectures, with code released for reproducibility. The method is model-agnostic: experiments show QDF improves various forecast models and achieves state-of-the-art results. The weighting matrix is learned adaptively rather than fixed, and the code is available at https://github.com/Master-PLC/QDF.

SORL aligns policy optimization with the turn structure of multi-turn interactions and adaptively suppresses unreliable off-policy updates, reducing gradient variance. The authors evaluate SO-PPO and SO-GRPO on open-domain QA, multi-hop QA, and medical multiple-choice QA, and test transfer to asynchronous RL for math reasoning by training on DAPO-Math-17k and validating on AIME-2024.

## [Goal-PD: Memory-Frugal Asynchronous Gossip Algorithm for Decentralized Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20571) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Goal-PD, an asynchronous gossip-based primal-dual algorithm for decentralized non-smooth convex optimization that maintains only two variables per node regardless of its degree, instead of the typical O(d) auxiliary variables. The paper proves almost-sure convergence to a minimizer and linear convergence for piecewise linear-quadratic objectives, and shows that pairwise averaging is a special case of Goal-PD, linking the primal-dual framework to classical gossip. This work significantly reduces memory requirements in decentralized learning, making it practical for dense networks and resource-constrained devices where stale information can otherwise degrade performance. The theoretical link to classical gossip averaging also provides a unified perspective that could influence future algorithm design in distributed optimization. Goal-PD achieves O(1) memory per node independent of degree, and experiments on synthetic and real datasets across various topologies with non-smooth objectives like median estimation show faster convergence than existing asynchronous baselines. The linear convergence guarantee is limited to piecewise linear-quadratic objectives, while almost-sure convergence holds more generally.

**Background**: Decentralized optimization allows multiple nodes to collaboratively solve a problem without a central server, often using gossip protocols where nodes exchange information with neighbors. Asynchronous algorithms let nodes operate at different speeds, but they often require extra memory per node proportional to its degree, which can be problematic in dense networks.

## [ReLoop Tackles Silent Failures in LLM-Generated Optimization Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15983) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReLoop introduces two mechanisms—structured generation via a four-stage reasoning chain (understand, formalize, synthesize, verify) and behavioral verification through solver-based parameter perturbation—to detect and reduce silent semantic errors in LLM-generated optimization code. It achieves +8.5pp accuracy on RetailOpt-190 with Claude Opus 4.6, +4.4pp on MAMO-ComplexLP for localized defects, and reaches 100% executable code with diagnostic execution recovery. LLM-generated optimization code often executes and returns solver-feasible solutions while encoding semantically incorrect formulations, with the feasibility-correctness gap reaching 90 percentage points on compositional problems. ReLoop's verification approach requires no ground truth, making it practical for real-world deployment where correct formulations are unknown, and it could improve reliability across supply chain, logistics, and operations research applications. The two mechanisms address different error structures: structured generation gives the largest gain on compositional problems, while behavioral verification gives its largest gain on localized defects. For a narrowly fine-tuned SFT model, the chain-of-thought prompt conflicts with its learned output format and lowers accuracy on MAMO-ComplexLP, an interaction the authors document and analyze. The paper also releases RetailOpt-190, a benchmark of 190 compositional retail optimization scenarios with interacting constraints.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models can translate natural-language problem descriptions into optimization code, but the generated code may contain silent failures—it runs and produces a solver-feasible answer while the underlying mathematical formulation is wrong. Such errors are hard to catch because the solver reports success, and traditional verification would require knowing the correct formulation in advance. ReLoop addresses this by decomposing code generation into explicit reasoning stages and by perturbing solver parameters to test whether the formulation responds correctly, a signal that comes from the solver rather than from LLM self-review.

A new arXiv paper (2603.04364v2) introduces Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training (DMAST), a three-stage framework that co-trains multimodal web agents and attackers as a two-player general-sum Markov game. On out-of-distribution tasks, DMAST nearly halves attack success rate (41.2% to 21.4%) while raising task completion by over 60% relative (6.2% to 10.2%), with code released on GitHub. Multimodal web agents that read both screenshots and accessibility trees are increasingly deployed for browser automation, and this work shows that injecting content into the DOM can corrupt both observation channels at once, a threat text-centric safety training largely ignores. By demonstrating genuine co-evolutionary robustness gains, DMAST offers a practical defense template for researchers and engineers building secure web automation and AI agents. DMAST uses a three-stage pipeline: imitation learning from a strong teacher model, oracle-guided supervised fine-tuning with a novel zero-acknowledgment strategy to keep reasoning task-focused under adversarial noise, and adversarial reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) self-play. The authors note it outperforms established training-based defenses and complements prompt-based defenses, though absolute task completion remains low at 10.2%.

## [PC-Diffuser Embeds Capsule CBF Safety Filter into Diffusion Trajectory Planner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10330) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PC-Diffuser introduces a safety augmentation framework that embeds a certifiable, path-consistent capsule control barrier function (CBF) directly into the denoising loop of diffusion-based trajectory planners. Rather than applying safety as a post-hoc fix, it evaluates collision risk via a capsule-distance barrier, converts denoised waypoints into kinematically feasible motion under a bicycle model, and applies a path-consistent safety filter at every denoising step. Diffusion-based planners show strong closed-loop driving performance but are hard to certify and can fail catastrophically in rare or out-of-distribution scenarios. By making safety intrinsic to trajectory generation, PC-Diffuser offers a path toward certifiable, distribution-preserving safety for learned planners in autonomous driving and robotics. The capsule-distance barrier better reflects vehicle geometry and reduces unnecessary conservativeness compared with simpler point-based barriers, while the safety filter eliminates residual constraint violations without geometric distortion so the corrected plan stays close to the learned distribution. Corrections are injected at every denoising step and the refined trajectory is fed back into the diffusion process for iterative, context-aware safeguarding.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Control barrier functions (CBFs) are mathematical tools that certify and enforce safety by keeping a system's state within a safe set, often used as safety filters on top of a nominal controller. Diffusion-based trajectory planners generate full-horizon driving plans by iteratively denoising random noise, learning multi-modal behavior from expert demonstrations. PC-Diffuser combines these two ideas so that safety constraints are enforced inside the diffusion denoising loop rather than after the plan is produced.

A new arXiv paper (2603.16017v2) introduces 'moral reasoning trajectories' — sequences of ethical framework invocations across intermediate reasoning steps — and analyzes them across six LLMs and three benchmarks. The authors empirically validate this on sentiment analysis and image classification tasks, and derive a theoretical bound showing that pure self-attention rank decays to one doubly exponentially with depth under Sinkhorn normalization. The paper confirms that, as previously shown for softmax attention, skip connections remain crucial for mitigating rank collapse even with Sinkhorn normalization. ## [PBT-Bench: A New Benchmark for AI Agents on Property-Based Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15229) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced PBT-Bench, a benchmark of 100 curated property-based testing problems spanning 40 real Python libraries, with 365 injected semantic bugs (mean 3.65 per problem) stratified into three difficulty levels. They evaluated eight contemporary LLMs under two prompting regimes, finding bug recall of 42.1%–83.4% with Hypothesis scaffolding versus 31.4%–76.7% in an open-ended baseline. Existing code benchmarks only check whether an agent can reproduce a known bug or write a patch, so they fail to isolate the distinct skill of deriving semantic invariants from documentation and designing input-generation strategies. PBT-Bench fills this gap, offering a resource for measuring documentation-grounded semantic reasoning in AI agents and revealing persistent, model-specific weaknesses. The injected bugs are designed so that default-strategy random inputs almost never trigger them, forcing agents to read library documentation and specify a Hypothesis @given strategy that concentrates input mass in the trigger region. Hypothesis scaffolding lifts mid-capability models by over 20 percentage points but yields smaller gains for the strongest models, with two exceptions showing degradation, and the hardest bugs prove model-specific.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Property-based testing is a technique where instead of writing individual example-based tests, you state a property that should hold for all inputs in a described range, and the testing library generates many random inputs to try to falsify it. Hypothesis is the leading property-based testing library for Python, and its @given decorator turns a test function into a randomized test driven by a strategy that controls how inputs are generated. A semantic invariant is a property that must remain true about a value, object, or behavior, and deriving such invariants from documentation is a key part of writing effective property-based tests.

## [SAE-Based Diagnosis of Over-Calling Bias in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18882) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.18882) diagnoses an intrinsic over-calling bias in LLM agents using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), showing that six models from three families achieve only 55%-70% overall accuracy on the When2Call benchmark due to much lower no-call accuracy. The authors propose Adaptive Margin-Calibrated Steering (AMCS), a closed-form counter-bias shift along SAE decoder directions that mitigates over-calling and improves overall accuracy with negligible loss in call accuracy. This work recasts over-calling from an empirical phenomenon into a mechanistic object amenable to causal correction, offering a principled path to improve tool-use reliability in LLM agents. Better no-call decisions could reduce unnecessary API costs, latency, and unsafe tool invocations in deployed agent systems. The Intrinsic Bias Hypothesis (IBH) posits an activation-independent call offset in the call/no-call decision mapping, so models favor calling even at activation parity; the model is decision-neutral only when no_call activation outweighs call activation. AMCS is a closed-form shift along SAE decoder directions, and code is available at https://github.com/SKURA502/agent-sae/, though validation is currently limited to the When2Call benchmark.

## [DAR: Distribution-Aware RL Objective Improves LLM Regression Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20740) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Distribution-Aware Reward (DAR), an on-policy reinforcement learning objective that jointly evaluates the empirical predictive distribution formed by multiple predictions for the same input, rather than scoring each prediction independently. To convert this distribution-level objective into rollout-level rewards, each prediction receives credit based on its leave-one-out contribution to the overall predictive distribution quality. Most LLM regression objectives optimize predictions independently, which often yields poor calibration of uncertainty estimates. DAR addresses this by encouraging predictions that are well-centered and appropriately dispersed around the target, which could improve reliability of LLM-based regression in scientific and engineering applications. DAR is evaluated on three regression settings: a synthetic task probing interpolation and extrapolation, and two real-world scientific tasks involving code and molecular data. Across tasks, it produces better-calibrated uncertainty estimates while consistently reducing prediction error and improving ranking quality over supervised fine-tuning and pointwise reinforcement learning.

**Background**: Large language models are increasingly used as flexible regressors that predict real-valued quantities from heterogeneous inputs, but standard training objectives treat each prediction independently. On-policy reinforcement learning trains a model using data generated by the current policy itself, and predictive distribution calibration refers to how well predicted uncertainty matches actual outcomes. Leave-one-out contribution is a technique that measures how much a single prediction affects the quality of the whole set, borrowed from cross-validation and contribution scoring.

## [Terminal Representation: A New Reward-Weighted Encoding for RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31289) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the terminal representation (TR), a new reward-weighted trajectory encoding in reinforcement learning that is structurally distinct from the successor representation (SR) and default representation (DR). The TR can be learned as a lower-dimensional object and used directly for option discovery, reward shaping, transfer learning, and exploration without computing eigenvectors. By avoiding eigendecomposition, the TR removes the assumption of symmetric transition dynamics and reduces the computational overhead of learning, storing, and using the representation. This could make representation-driven downstream tasks in RL more practical and broadly applicable. The paper develops the theoretical foundations of the TR, including its derivation, convergence of two learning algorithms, zero-shot compositionality, and equivalences between alternative reward formulations. It further shows that the TR is embedded in the top DR eigenvector, allowing it to capture the same underlying knowledge without eigendecomposition, and provides empirical evidence of its viability with less computational overhead.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: In reinforcement learning, representation learning helps agents abstract over space and time. The successor representation (SR) encodes states by the future trajectories they induce, capturing information flow decoupled from reward, while the default representation (DR) builds on this by weighting trajectories with reward to integrate credit-assignment structure. Eigenvectors of both representations have been used for downstream tasks such as option discovery, reward shaping, transfer learning, and exploration, but eigendecomposition imposes a symmetric transition dynamics assumption and adds computational cost.

## [Banyan Study: Task Diversity Aids Transfer but Hinders Continual RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00880) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Banyan, a GPU-accelerated continual reinforcement learning domain that lets researchers parametrically control three independent axes of task diversity: map layouts, interactable objects, and hierarchical sub-goal dependency structures. Experiments show that increasing diversity along each axis produces systematic transfer, but excessive diversity inhibits a learner's ability to keep adapting to new task distributions. The findings reveal a fundamental tension between transfer and continual learning, challenging the assumption that more task diversity is always better for adaptive agents. This has practical implications for designing training curricula and benchmarks for agents that must keep learning over sequences of distribution shifts. The phenomenon holds across different continual learning algorithms, memory architectures, and architecture sizes, and also appears in Kinetix, a physics-based control domain. Notably, as diversity increases, learners plateau on new tasks yet keep improving on old tasks even without further exposure to them; Banyan's code is released on GitHub.

How task diversity affects an agent's ability to keep learning across distribution shifts remained unclear.

## [FFR Extends Forward-Forward Learning to Regression Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03927) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose FFR (Forward-Forward for Regression), the first framework to extend Hinton's Forward-Forward algorithm to real-world regression, introducing an ordinal competitive goodness function, a stratified ladder architecture, and hierarchical prediction with uncertainty estimation. Experiments on six real-world regression benchmarks show FFR recovers on average 98.5% of backpropagation's accuracy while cutting peak training memory to 27% at depth 8 and 8% at depth 32. This addresses a fundamental limitation of the Forward-Forward algorithm, which was inherently designed for classification via contrastive positive-negative pairs and could not handle continuous target spaces. By making FF viable for regression, FFR broadens the applicability of biologically plausible, backpropagation-free learning to tasks like forecasting and scientific modeling, potentially inspiring further research into local learning methods. FFR replaces contrastive pairs with competitive learning between partitioned neuron groups under distance-aware ordinal supervision, uses a stratified ladder where shallow layers learn coarse ordinal discrimination and deeper layers refine fine-grained regression, and provides a single-pass uncertainty score. Per-iteration time is about 72% of backpropagation's, and FFR substantially outperforms all BP-free competitors.

**Background**: The Forward-Forward algorithm, introduced by Geoffrey Hinton in 2022, is an alternative to backpropagation that trains neural networks through two forward passes (one with positive data, one with negative data) using purely local, layer-wise optimization, making it more biologically plausible and memory-efficient. However, it was designed for classification and relies on contrastive positive-negative sample pairs, which do not naturally exist in continuous regression problems. Biologically plausible learning research seeks training methods that avoid backpropagation's global error signals, which are considered implausible in real brains.

## [Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces and Its Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06840) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2606.06840v2) mechanistically analyzes how reasoning-trained language models perform zero-shot multi-label tasks over thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidate labels, using attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in, and null calibration to give individual attention heads causal standing. It introduces MISTILL, a distillation method that supervises the student's pooled attention at decision events rather than only transferring the teacher's reasoning text. The work connects mechanistic interpretability with knowledge distillation, showing that a small, phase-structured set of attention heads is both necessary and sufficient for correct decisions on essentially every clinical summary. This suggests interpretability findings can be turned into practical training signals, potentially improving smaller or cross-family student models on high-stakes tasks like clinical coding. On MIMIC-IV clinical coding with all 5,651 candidate diagnosis codes in context, distinct head families attend to the candidate region and back to a near-miss named earlier, and the region can be elicited several tokens before the code from a disjoint mid-layer set. MISTILL nearly doubles causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference under bf16 weights but a task cost with fp32 master weights.

The paper introduces support-conditioned control-sensitivity regularization, a method that promotes local responsiveness to control input changes in well-supported training regions of learned dynamics models. Experiments in vision-based obstacle avoidance, manipulation, and real-robot navigation show improved out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and safer closed-loop planning. The regularization preserves control-induced variation while limiting unstable extrapolation due to weak empirical support, and the high-support set is periodically updated as the encoder evolves during training. ## [Prime Fourier Embeddings Encode Integers for Modular Arithmetic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23044) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce Prime Fourier Embeddings (PFE), which encode integers as prime-indexed (cos, sin) pairs derived from harmonic analysis of the rational numbers Q. They prove that any linear map equivariant under the product group action must be block-diagonal with one independent block per prime, a result following from Schur's lemma, and confirm empirically that task-relevant channels specialize by over 500x with perfect in-distribution accuracy on all square-free composite moduli tested. This work provides a principled theoretical framework for neural embeddings of integers, potentially improving how models learn structured representations and perform modular arithmetic tasks. It bridges representation theory and deep learning, offering a mathematically grounded alternative to discovering algebraic structure from scratch. The approach leverages the Chinese Remainder Theorem to predict which prime channels are task-relevant for square-free composite moduli, and ablation studies show specialization ratios exceeding 500x between relevant and irrelevant channels. The theoretical guarantees rely on Schur's lemma applied to the character decomposition of the product group action.

## [Variational-Ising-Attention Tailors Softmax for Scientific Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23634) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Variational-Ising-Attention (VIA), which augments standard softmax attention with an interacting Ising model whose pairwise couplings are learned via variational mean-field inference. VIA is instantiated on retrosynthesis reaction center prediction and, as an internal ablation, protein residue contact prediction, substantially outperforming standard softmax attention across model variants. This work challenges the prevailing assumption that attention should prioritize sparsity and efficiency, arguing that scientific tasks with cooperative constraints benefit from richer structured coupling. If validated, it could shift attention design for domains like chemistry and biology toward domain-tailored mechanisms rather than general-purpose efficiency. VIA extends attention from a ranking over isolated items to a collective state over interacting entities, with attention patterns emerging from learnable pairwise couplings. The abstract is truncated and no community discussion is provided, so independent replication and full experimental details remain to be seen.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Softmax attention computes query-key scores and normalizes them independently, which implicitly assumes items are unrelated. The Ising model is a classic statistical physics model of coupled binary spins, often used to study phase transitions and cooperative phenomena. Variational mean-field inference approximates intractable posteriors with fully factorized distributions, enabling tractable learning of coupling parameters. Retrosynthesis reaction center prediction identifies which bonds break in a chemical reaction, while protein contact prediction estimates which residues are spatially close.

## [Study finds no uniform AI deficit in extreme weather forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09972) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2608.09972v2) evaluates twelve physical and AI forecast models against ECMWF IFS using ten months of European station observations, covering 10 m wind, 2 m temperature, solar radiation, and precipitation. It finds no uniform AI-specific deficit in the tails: some AI models outperform IFS under extreme conditions while others deteriorate markedly, with similar variation among physical models. The results challenge the widely repeated claim that AI weather models systematically underestimate extremes, suggesting that tail performance depends on the model, variable, and evaluation setting rather than on whether the forecast is AI or physical. This matters for how forecasters, researchers, and policymakers judge the readiness of AI models for high-impact weather prediction. The evaluation uses station observations rather than reanalysis for verification and defines regimes from a fixed ERA5 1991-2020 climatology, addressing the common criticism that earlier evidence relied on deterministic regression models verified against reanalysis. Notably, every model shows a common conditional-error pattern, overpredicting low observations and underpredicting high ones, so attenuation of extremes does not imply a uniform loss of relative skill.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) is a global numerical weather prediction system jointly developed by ECMWF and Météo-France, widely regarded as a leading baseline for forecast skill. ERA5 is ECMWF's fifth-generation atmospheric reanalysis, providing a consistent historical record from 1940 onward that is often used to define climatological regimes. AI weather models, typically trained as deterministic regression models on such reanalysis data, have recently achieved forecast skill comparable to numerical weather prediction at far lower computational cost, but their reliability for extremes has remained largely uncharacterized.

## [Cost-Aware Hierarchical Multi-Agent System Cuts Ransomware Analysis Costs by 44.6%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04820) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.04820v2) introduces a cost-aware Hierarchical Multi-Agent System (HMAS) that treats evidence acquisition as a budgeted sequential decision problem, starting with static analysis and escalating to dynamic and memory forensics only when confidence is insufficient or agents disagree. Across 12,439 samples from 16 ransomware families plus benign files, the deterministic HMAS achieved F1 0.93 and macro F1 0.97 while resolving 57.95% of cases with static evidence alone and reducing average internal analysis cost from 12 to 6.65 units, a 44.6% reduction. Multimodal ransomware detectors typically run every analysis modality on every sample, so cost and time-to-verdict grow linearly with sample volume even when static evidence already suffices. This work shows that a tiered, budget-aware escalation policy can preserve high detection accuracy while substantially cutting the expensive sandbox and memory-forensics resources that bottleneck security operations centers. The architecture uses specialist agents that emit schema-validated risk signals per modality, domain controllers that aggregate them, and a Meta-Orchestrator that escalates only on low confidence or intra-controller disagreement; an optional locally hosted LLM reviewer can shift a verdict by at most one tier but cannot override the deterministic pipeline, and every decision carries a full provenance trace. A key caveat is generalization: in leave-one-family-out testing, accuracy on held-out families drops to 0.26–0.64 outside the Benign and high-support classes.

**Background**: Ransomware triage relies on three main evidence sources: static analysis, which inspects file structure and code without executing it and scales to millions of files; dynamic (sandbox) analysis, which runs the sample to observe behavior; and memory forensics, which examines live RAM to uncover runtime artifacts that malware hides from disk. Dynamic and memory analysis are far more expensive, requiring minutes of analyst-controlled infrastructure per sample, which is why deciding when to escalate is a resource-allocation problem. Hierarchical multi-agent systems organize AI agents into tiers where higher-level agents delegate focused subtasks to lower-level ones, a design pattern increasingly used to manage complex analysis workflows.

## [SpliTEE Combines GPU-Assisted TEEs and Differential Privacy for Fast Private LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15039) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SpliTEE extends the Slalom split-inference architecture to large language models by protecting intermediate representations with differential privacy instead of encryption, and contributes a global sensitivity analysis of key LLM functions that bounds the required DP noise scale. Implemented on Intel TDX with Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen3-4B, the split execution is nearly twice as fast as fully TDX-based inference and up to 43% faster than Slalom while achieving higher accuracy. Private LLM inference is a critical bottleneck for deploying models on sensitive user data, and TEE-only execution is too slow because current TEEs are CPU-based while LLM inference is GPU-optimized. By showing that DP can replace encryption for outsourced intermediate computations without quantization, SpliTEE offers a practical path to faster privacy-preserving inference that should interest both privacy-preserving ML and systems security researchers. The paper first demonstrates that masking intermediate representations is necessary by achieving 80% accuracy on a prompt-reconstruction attack from those representations. It also derives an upper bound on floating-point error from masking and subsequent noise cancellation as a function of the privacy parameter epsilon, and shows that prompt reconstruction, even with knowledge of the DP mechanism, cannot recover more information than an unrelated prompt.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: A trusted execution environment (TEE) is a secure area of a main processor, such as Intel TDX or AMD SEV, that protects code and data with confidentiality and integrity even from the cloud provider. Differential privacy (DP) is a formal privacy notion in which a randomized algorithm's output is guaranteed to be nearly indistinguishable whether or not any single input is included, with the privacy budget epsilon controlling the trade-off between privacy and utility. Slalom, proposed by Tramèr and Boneh in 2019, splits neural network inference between a TEE and an untrusted GPU and encrypts the intermediate inputs sent to the GPU; SpliTEE adapts this idea to LLMs but replaces encryption with DP.

## [Local Sparsity Enables Unsupervised LLM Safety Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20129) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.20129v2) proposes a locally masked sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based anomaly detection framework for unsupervised LLM safety, exploiting the insight that under the linear representation hypothesis (LRH), nearby points in the SAE concept space share a small common active support. The authors provide theoretical justifications and validate the approach across multiple architectures and datasets, including capability-testing and safety-specific benchmarks, showing that with only 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal performance while using just 1-2% of SAE neurons. Deployment-time LLM safety methods are predominantly supervised and assume access to unsafe training data, which cannot anticipate new attacks or harm categories. This work reframes safety as anomaly detection over safe data only, potentially enabling more robust and adaptable deployment-time safeguards that generalize to unseen threats while remaining computationally cheap. The framework relies on the linear representation hypothesis and sparse autoencoders to recover an interpretable concept space, where local sparsity means nearby activations share few active features. A key caveat is that near-optimal performance requires allowing the algorithm to use 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, and the method only activates 1-2% of SAE neurons, which raises questions about coverage of rare harm categories.

**Background**: The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) posits that high-level concepts in LLMs are encoded as linear directions in activation space, which has become a foundational idea in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are unsupervised tools that decompose LLM activations into sparse, interpretable features, often used to extract concept directions from models like GPT-4. Anomaly detection flags inputs that deviate from a model of normal (safe) data, and this paper combines these ideas by using local sparsity in SAE feature space to detect unsafe or out-of-distribution prompts without labeled unsafe data.

## [ValueDiff: Value-Geometric KV Cache Eviction for Sink-Suppressed LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23314) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ValueDiff introduces a value-geometric KV cache eviction method that ranks tokens by the L2 deviation of their value vectors from the cache mean, rather than relying on attention scores. On RULER at a 2k token budget it retains 88-99% of dense performance across seven sink-suppressed models (best on 6 of 7), and on LongBench at 4k it averages 92% retention versus 83% for the strongest prior baseline. Many modern LLMs use QK-normalization, gated attention, learned attention sinks, or logit softcapping, which weaken the persistent attention sinks that existing eviction methods depend on. ValueDiff offers a query-invariant signal that works reliably for these architectures, potentially improving memory efficiency and long-context inference for a growing class of models. The same score arises as the minimal-disturbance eviction under a max-entropy assumption about future attention, and evaluation uses fixed cache budgets with eviction at every block boundary during prefill and every decoding step during generation. On MATH-500 at a 25% cache budget, ValueDiff is the strongest non-dense method on every sink-suppressed model tested, outperforming prior methods by up to ~20 points on gated-attention models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: KV cache stores key and value vectors for all previously processed tokens so that LLMs can generate text without recomputing the entire context, but its memory grows linearly with sequence length and becomes a bottleneck for long-context inference. KV cache eviction reduces this memory by discarding less important tokens, and most existing methods decide importance using attention scores. Attention sinks are tokens that attract a disproportionate share of attention mass, and many eviction methods implicitly rely on them; however, newer architectures with QK-normalization, gated attention, learned sinks, or logit softcapping exhibit weaker sinks, undermining those methods.

## [KernelOPT: Dispatch-Aware Multi-Agent LLM System for GPU Kernel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30059) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KernelOPT introduces a multi-agent LLM system that treats compiled models as structured artifacts, preserving vendor library calls (cuBLAS, cuDNN) while exclusively optimizing compiler-generated Triton sub-kernels via five profiling-guided LLM agents. Evaluated on 250 KernelBench problems on NVIDIA H200, it achieves geometric mean speedups over torch.compile of 1.40x (Level 1), 1.15x (Level 2), and 1.07x (Level 3), with optimized-only geomeans reaching 2.54x, 1.84x, and 1.37x respectively. Existing LLM-assisted kernel optimizers treat compiled models as black boxes and optimize standalone kernels without respecting compiler structural decisions or verifying end-to-end model correctness, leaving a significant gap in practical deployment. KernelOPT's dispatch-aware approach that preserves vendor library calls and verifies model-level performance could make LLM-driven kernel optimization viable for real-world PyTorch models, directly benefiting deep learning inference and training efficiency. The system uses a four-gate verification cascade: static validation, multi-seed correctness checking, model-level float64-fallback verification, and performance gating (gamma=1.03), and preserves the compiler baseline when candidates fail verification. It accepts PyTorch nn Modules, standalone Triton kernels, and Helion kernels, though the abstract is truncated and the optimized-only speedups apply to only a subset of problems (36/100 L1, 23/100 L2, 11/50 L3).

## [Paper Names the 'Authorship Hazard' in Agentic Dataspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30614) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An arXiv paper (2609.30614v2) introduces the 'authorship hazard': LLM agents that both author and are subject to governance policies can undermine authorization. Across 90 preregistered edits to a running agreement, each evaluated on 344,512 requests, six edits that only reclassify a field all changed authorization and narrowed a duty without touching policy text, and a policy-diff classifier passed all six. The finding matters because it shows that seemingly innocuous field reclassifications can silently alter what an agent is authorized to do, undermining governance in multi-agent and dataspace settings. It argues for a strict principle that an agent is a subject of the governance plane, never an author of it, with implications for AI safety, compliance, and enterprise agent deployment. Read as worded, the privilege-delta conditions pass 33 of 69 effective policy-text edits, but read as covering any relaxation, none pass; treating classification as authorship routes all six reclassifications to review, though the required registry is not yet built. At the execution boundary, protected fields reach the model in 105 of 105 cases under prompt-stated duties and in 0 of 105 under a compiled tool-call constraint, while values outside named fields are exposed in 7 of 7 cases.

## [LLM-Developed Local Infrared Subtraction for Collider Calculations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36007) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.36007v3) presents AI-developed local infrared subtraction schemes in which an LLM, under human physics guidance, produces two implementations: a neural-network phase-space projection that fits the Born contact by matching EFT cumulants, and an analytic construction that keeps Born momenta fixed while integrating over radiation. The authors reconstruct the full NLO correction for massless 3- and 4-jet production in electron-positron annihilation and make a first attempt at NNLO dijet production, with results in good agreement with EERAD3. Infrared subtraction is a long-standing bottleneck for higher-order QCD calculations at colliders such as the LHC, and this work suggests that LLMs guided by physicists can help construct subtraction schemes that avoid slicing parameters while reusing existing lower-order radiation and EFT singular predictions. If validated, this could accelerate the development of NNLO and beyond-NNLO tools and strengthen the case for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The framework separates an integrable radiation term from a finite Born contact determined by the EFT singular distribution in an N-jettiness resolution observable, yielding a local subtraction formula without a slicing parameter. Notably, the numerical calculation and projection-network training were performed on a 2020 Apple M1 MacBook without GPU acceleration, and the appendices extend the local subtraction to 3-jet NNLO with explicit radiation maps and a proposed contact formula.

**Background**: In perturbative QCD, fixed-order calculations of jet cross sections suffer from infrared divergences when emitted gluons become soft or collinear, and subtraction schemes cancel these divergences by adding and subtracting approximate counterterms. Effective field theory provides singular distributions that capture the soft and collinear behavior, and this paper uses those predictions as input for AI-generated subtraction terms.

## [Cross-Model LLM Review Detects More Planted Errors Than Same-Model Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01471) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A controlled arXiv preprint (2610.01471v2) reports an experiment with 30 artifacts, 150 planted errors, 10 review conditions, and 900 review sessions using three reviewer models from two developers. It finds that a top-tier cross-model reviewer alone is not significantly different in F1 from same-model review in a fresh session, but combining one same-model review with one cross-model review detects more planted errors (56.7% vs. 42.7%) than two same-model reviews. This provides practical, statistically grounded guidance for teams using LLMs to verify code, documentation, and analyses: simply swapping in a stronger model may not help, but pairing same-model and cross-model reviews can improve error detection. It also cautions that model difference and reviewer capability are not separated in the experiment, so the source of the gain remains unclear. The two review types find partly different errors (Jaccard 41.2%), and a lightweight cross-model reviewer scores no higher than same-model review. Withholding requirements raises F1 for the two lower tiers but not the top tier, and the results depend on how failed sessions are scored; one baseline run of uncertain provenance and 14 failed calls were excluded before analysis.

**Background**: Large language models are increasingly used not only to generate code and documentation but also to review such output, and a common question is whether a second review by a different model adds value. This study builds on earlier preprints that varied context, repetition, and role structure within a single model, and now tests model independence. F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, Jaccard similarity measures overlap between two sets of detected errors, and the Holm-Bonferroni method adjusts p-values for multiple comparisons.

## [Completion Aware Guidance Boosts World Action Model Task Success](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01559) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), a training-free sampling method that steers World Action Models (WAMs) toward task-completing transitions rather than merely plausible local continuations. Across representative WAMs, CAG raises success from 64% to 70% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation, while cutting task-incomplete imagination from 79% to 40%. Task-incomplete imagination is a known failure mode in embodied AI, where a world model predicts a plausible future that never actually finishes the task. A training-free fix that works across existing WAMs could be widely adopted in robotics research without retraining or architectural changes. The authors show the failure is not inherent to the world model backbone but emerges when WAMs are adapted for short-chunk control, which repeatedly favors plausible local continuations over task-completing transitions. CAG is a sampling-time intervention, so it adds no training cost, though the reported gains are evaluated on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and simulation rather than real-world hardware.

A new arXiv paper introduces Sparse Asymmetric Group-Query Attention (SAGA), which decouples key and value head counts so that fewer key heads are used while more value heads are retained, paired with an approximate top-N (Atop-N) sparse attention method. Together they achieve end-to-end decoding speedups exceeding 2x over a full-attention GQA baseline at long contexts, and the authors also provide a fine-tuning method to convert pretrained models to the SAGA architecture without costly retraining. Attention is the main bottleneck in autoregressive LLM decoding, so a method that cuts decoding latency by more than 2x while nearly matching GQA quality could directly benefit anyone serving or deploying LLMs. The fine-tuning conversion path is especially important because it lets practitioners adopt SAGA on existing pretrained models rather than training from scratch. The core observation is that in sparse attention the probability-value multiplication becomes negligible, shifting the bottleneck to the query-key step, so key heads can be reduced while extra value heads preserve capacity at limited decoding cost. The work formalizes the benefits of this asymmetry theoretically and validates them empirically with latency and quality evaluations on models up to 1.5B parameters.

The study introduces the Shortest Matching Sequence (SMS), an alignment scheme that maps between the word segmentation used by eye-tracking corpora and the subword tokenization of language models, which often disagree in Mandarin Chinese. Using Chinese-Pythia models (14M–1.4B parameters) trained from scratch on 30B tokens, the authors find that LM surprisal predicts first fixation duration, gaze duration, and total reading time in three Mandarin eye-tracking corpora (GECO-CN, HKP, MECO), contrary to previous null findings. This work challenges earlier null results and shows that LM surprisal is a viable predictor of Chinese reading behavior, which matters for both psycholinguistic theories of sentence processing and the evaluation of language models on Chinese. It also warns that scaling conclusions drawn from a single eye-tracking corpus may not generalize, since predictive power scaled positively in GECO-CN but inversely in HKP and, at the largest sizes, in MECO. The inverse scaling in HKP appears linked to checkpoints whose surprisal stays closer to n-gram statistics, which turn out to be better predictors of reading; the authors therefore caution against drawing scaling conclusions from a single corpus. The SMS alignment is necessary because eye-tracking corpora assume word segmentation while LMs use subword tokenization, and the two tokenizations frequently disagree in Mandarin Chinese.

## [E²-OPSD Fixes Entropy Overshoot in On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05048) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.05048v3) identifies an 'entropy overshoot' failure mode in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), where student token entropy rises above the teacher's and stays elevated, and proposes E²-OPSD to fix it. E²-OPSD combines exemplar-guided teaching, which replaces the current answer with a retrieved solved neighboring problem, and entropy-aware distillation, which uses the student-teacher entropy gap to set the direction and strength of each token's correction, improving math reasoning by up to 4.3 points in mean@16 over OPSD. On-policy self-distillation is an increasingly popular way to give LLMs dense token-level supervision without training a separate teacher model, so a systematic failure mode like entropy overshoot could silently degrade many self-distillation pipelines. E²-OPSD's targeted fix improves in-domain math reasoning and also generalizes out of domain, with gains up to 4.9 points in mean@16 and 5.5 points in pass@8 over base models, while adding no extra forward passes or networks. The paper traces entropy overshoot to two causes: the reference-conditioned teacher is confident along its own answer-directed reasoning path but transfers that confidence poorly to student-generated prefixes, and the forward KL used by OPSD continually diffuses the student's predictive distribution without pulling it back. E²-OPSD remains simple, requiring no additional forward passes or networks, though the reported gains are measured on math reasoning benchmarks and the approach is an incremental methodological advance rather than a paradigm shift.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a training recipe in which a single network acts as both teacher, conditioned on a reference solution, and student, conditioned only on the problem, providing dense token-level supervision without a second model. Entropy in this context measures the uncertainty of the model's next-token predictive distribution; when student entropy drifts too high, the model's outputs become noisy and less reliable. Forward KL divergence is a common distillation loss that penalizes the student for assigning low probability to tokens the teacher favors, and prior work has debated forward versus reverse KL for LLM distillation.

Researchers from KAIST's AI Lab propose Best-of-N Guidance (BoNG), a method that performs online Best-of-N selection over denoising particles and injects an asymmetric guidance interaction during the reverse diffusion process. ## [Incentive Alignment in Online Experimentation via Sample Splitting and Shrinkage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05922) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.05922v2) reframes online experimentation as an incentive design problem, showing that two practical mechanisms—sample splitting and shrinkage—can align decentralized experimenters' incentives with platform value. Sample splitting achieves perfect incentive alignment at a bounded traffic cost, while shrinkage requires no additional traffic and guarantees that interventions with negative expected effects are strictly unprofitable to field. This work addresses a structural principal-agent conflict in A/B testing that conventional centralized levers like significance thresholds and traffic budgets cannot resolve, potentially eroding platform value. It offers both researchers and practitioners a theoretically grounded, practical framework for improving experimentation governance in large online platforms. The paper models experimentation as a principal-agent problem where experimenters choose hypotheses and are rewarded based on empirically biased average treatment effects. Sample splitting perfectly aligns incentives but incurs a bounded traffic cost, whereas shrinkage consumes no extra traffic and makes negative-expected-effect interventions strictly unprofitable.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Online platforms rely on A/B tests to evaluate whether new features causally improve metrics, but experimentation is operationally decentralized: the same experimenters who build features also decide what to test. Because they are typically rewarded for showing positive average treatment effects, they have an incentive to select and report biased results, a classic principal-agent problem. Recent literature has focused on centralized portfolio optimization to handle limited testing traffic, but this abstracts away the decentralized institutional reality. Sample splitting partitions data to align incentives, while shrinkage estimators deliberately introduce bias to reduce variance and discourage negative-value interventions.

TAPDreamer introduces a transferable adversarial patch attack against world action models that uses only a public encoder to craft a fixed local perturbation, requiring no queries to the target policy. In closed-loop evaluation, a single frozen patch covering about 6.5% of the input drops FastWAM's success rate from 97.7% to 0.0% on 40 LIBERO tasks and from 90.86% to 0.0% on 50 RoboTwin tasks, while matched random patches retain 81.5% and 79.2% success. This work shows that protecting downstream action generation alone is insufficient, since shared visual encoders are a single point of failure that can be attacked once and reused across tasks and architectures. It has direct implications for AI safety and robotics, where world action models are increasingly used for general-purpose robotic control. The attack's key insight is that interactions between patch-induced changes in attention weights and value vectors broadcast a nearly identical representation shift far beyond the patch footprint, and this shift remains stable across task observations. TAPDreamer uses six frames from one source task to maximize the global L1 distance between clean and patched encoder representations, and the same patches also reduce success to 1.45% and 1.00% on two DreamWAM configurations and to 10.60% on Motus.

## [Higher forecast coverage can worsen route decisions, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06995) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper empirically evaluates whether better traffic forecast coverage improves route decisions using a frozen protocol on processed road speed data from Beijing and Chengdu, with 150 origin-destination pairs, three candidate paths, and 14 test days per city. Joint upper-bound coverage rises from 83.19% to 92.26% in Beijing M1, from 75.14% to 88.33% in Chengdu M1, and from 74.01% to 90.64% in Chengdu M2, yet lateness increases by 0.1633, 0.7848, and 0.9200 percentage points respectively, and mean travel time rises by 0.588, 3.082, and 4.418 seconds. This finding challenges the common assumption that improving uncertainty coverage in traffic forecasting directly translates into better downstream route choices, suggesting that coverage metrics are not a reliable surrogate for route utility. It has implications for transportation researchers and practitioners who design forecasting systems and route recommendation algorithms, warning that optimizing coverage alone may degrade real-world travel outcomes. The study uses a frozen protocol that separates speed error, joint candidate-path upper-bound coverage, route selection, and realized loss, comparing raw 90th percentile path time bounds with jointly calibrated upper bounds under minimum bound route choice. In a separate Chengdu predictor comparison, a 14.91% reduction in speed mean absolute error accompanies a 1.4571 percentage point reduction in lateness under C0, and the authors caution that the offline results do not establish online or causal benefits.

**Background**: Traffic forecasting models often produce uncertainty intervals, and coverage measures how often the true value falls within the predicted bounds. ## [SPL Enables Multi-Agent RL with Staggered Agent Participation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07578) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07578v1) proposes Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning where some agents act earlier and leave information useful to agents that join later. SPL combines prospective acquisition supervision for early agents with outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents, and across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone-setting comparisons it improved observed mean task completion in every case, with an average gain of 14.1%. Most cooperative MARL research assumes agents participate concurrently, so this work formalizes a more realistic staggered participation setting where early actions matter through the information they pass on rather than only through immediate rewards. The reported gains across multiple backbones, eight-agent teams, and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab suggest the approach could generalize to real-world embodied and robotics tasks with asynchronous team formation. The core challenge is a cross-time, cross-agent learning dependency: an early action affects the return both through the information it provides and through the later policy that consumes it, so learning must identify useful information and teach later agents to use it. SPL is a training-time augmentation evaluated on policy-based MARL backbones, and the authors report consistent improvements across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings.

## [Study Finds Systematic Bias in 3D Mitochondrial Volume Measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07582) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint empirically assesses representation bias, correction transfer, and resolution sensitivity in three-dimensional mitochondrial morphometry, finding that occupancy-derived volumes exceed reference mesh volumes by 3.665% on average despite an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.994. Removing a depth offset in a controlled label-pipeline reimplementation reduces volume error by a mean of 1.57 percentage points, and a frozen regression reduces median absolute percentage error from 3.481% to 0.664% in 2,728 previously unused objects. This work provides quantitative checks that help researchers distinguish processing-induced descriptor changes from genuine biological differences in mitochondrial imaging, which is critical for the reliability of quantitative imaging pipelines used in biomedical research. It also shows that accuracy and uncertainty transfer must be evaluated separately, since the calibrated error bound covered only 92.1% overall and 49.2% in a low-occupancy subgroup. The study used 2,720 development objects from the 3D Mitochondria Shape Library for Optical Microscopy and 550 rat-cortex objects from the MitoEM resource; coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nanometers changed median surface area by minus 10.60% and sphericity by plus 11.76% despite a rank correlation of 0.994. The authors note that the source of the remaining volume inflation after removing the depth offset was not isolated, and the results do not establish biological invariance or cross-source correction transfer.

## [SUTURE: Structured Rollout-Group Verification for Video Temporal Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07601) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces SUTURE, a verifier for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) that conditions scoring on the entire rollout group rather than scoring each rollout independently. It shows the verifier admits an exact decomposition into a standard IoU term plus a covariance correction determined by the rollout group, and reports improved grounding performance across five temporal grounding benchmarks at every reported IoU threshold. Most RLVR overlap verifiers treat rollouts independently, discarding the joint structure that group-based methods like GRPO already exploit; SUTURE shows this structure can be turned into a more informative reward signal. If it generalizes, it could improve how pretrained video-language models are adapted to temporal grounding and reduce common failure modes such as anchoring predictions near the video start. The method operates at two scales: disagreement across rollouts controls how strongly the target is reweighted, while coverage at each position determines where reward mass is redistributed. A local gradient diagnostic reveals a preference for responses covering relatively less-supported target regions, and the trained policy shows less video-start anchoring, with the first temporal mention more often overlapping the annotated target for later events.

**Background**: Video temporal grounding (VTG) is the task of locating the video segment that matches a natural-language query, and its outputs are typically timestamped intervals. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) fine-tunes models using automatic, rule-based checkers instead of learned reward models, and for VTG the natural checker is intersection over union (IoU), the ratio of overlap to union between a predicted interval and the ground-truth interval. Group-based RL methods such as GRPO sample multiple rollouts per prompt and compare them, but existing overlap verifiers still score each rollout in isolation.

It also highlights that evaluation methodology choices can silently reverse benchmark results, affecting how the community compares quantized models. On tasks both variants complete without faults under the same prompt, the 8-bit minus 4-bit difference ranges from 0 to +20.2 percentage points for Llama and from -50.0 to +35.0 points for Qwen; full-pipeline point estimates favor 8-bit Llama under all five prompts, while the Qwen comparison changes direction across prompts. Executor leniency is identified as a third design choice that can reverse conclusions, and the authors recommend comparing variants on matched tasks, reporting full-pipeline success for deployment decisions, stating the scoring policy, and quantifying uncertainty across tasks rather than injected fault sites.

## [OSFP4 jointly optimizes diagonal smoothing and block scales for NVFP4 quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08231) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces OSFP4 (Optimized Smoothing and Scaling for NVFP4), a quantization scheme that jointly optimizes a diagonal smoothing matrix and NVFP4 block scales for each linear projection. It minimizes squared matrix-product quantization error under either round-to-nearest or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation rounding, and achieves the highest average accuracy among evaluated competitors while retaining roughly 94-97% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput. NVFP4 is a hardware-accelerated 4-bit format on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, and preserving LLM accuracy at such low precision is a key bottleneck for cheap, fast inference. OSFP4 shows that smarter post-training quantization can close much of the accuracy gap without sacrificing the tensor-core throughput that makes NVFP4 attractive, which matters to anyone deploying large models on Blackwell-class hardware. The joint optimization is made tractable by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer instead of the fixed deterministic one, and the code is released at https://github.com/neriahbd/OSFP4. The reported throughput retention of 94-97% is measured on specific workloads, so real-world gains may vary with model architecture and batch size.

**Background**: NVFP4 is a microscaling format introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell: each value is stored in FP4 E2M1, with one FP8 E4M3 scale per 16-value block and one FP32 scale per tensor, which reduces quantization error versus coarser 4-bit schemes. Post-training quantization methods such as GPTQ use approximate second-order information to round weights with minimal error, and smoothing techniques rescale activations or weights to make them easier to quantize. OSFP4 combines these ideas by learning a per-projection diagonal smoothing matrix together with the NVFP4 block scales.

The paper introduces Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD), a method that separates normalized execution relevance (relative transition support) from an effective pseudo-count mass, then uses a Dirichlet posterior to produce an uncertainty-penalized weight for KL-anchored correction learning. By showing that separating evidence support from evidence mass improves probability estimation and correction learning, it offers a principled uncertainty-aware alternative to fixed-weight self-distillation, relevant to researchers building agents that iteratively revise code. Under a symmetric prior, changing the mass preserves category ordering, and the effective mass yields a supervised coefficient bounded by its matched fixed-mass counterpart; in the primary matched DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, argmax predictions agree on all 3,000 examples, with the largest NLL gain under concentrated relevance.
