The paper proposes 'Anchor and Adapt,' a two-stage prompt learning framework that separates the acquisition of anomaly semantics from adaptation to target normal appearance. Stage I learns transferable normal and abnormal anchors from annotated auxiliary data, while Stage II keeps these anchors fixed and adapts an additional normal branch using only a few target normal samples. This approach reduces the need for manually specified, product-specific anomaly descriptions and avoids synthetic anomaly generation, which could make few-shot industrial anomaly detection more practical for fast manufacturing changeovers. It is relevant to automated inspection systems that must operate in data-scarce environments. The inherited and adapted normal branches jointly characterize target normality, with text-anchor regularization encouraging consistency with the generic normal prior and separation from the abnormal anchors. Cross-dataset experiments between MVTec-AD and VisA under 1-, 2-, and 4-shot settings show competitive detection and localization performance, and controlled ablations assess the roles of transferred anchors, asymmetric adaptation, dual-normal representations, and anchor regularization.

The framework injects faults into ReRAM crossbar arrays after mapping CNN learning parameters, and analyzes the impact of SaH and SaL fault models across different layers and parameter locations. The results show that vulnerability is greatly influenced by the types and depth of layers, the location of the learning parameter in each layer, and the value and type of faults, with SaL reducing classification accuracy more than SaH.

This confidence status gates automated enforcement: only corroborated intelligence is eligible for automated action, while lower-confidence objects are routed to analyst review or kept as context. A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.07340) introduces CausalBind, a causal modeling framework that identifies sparse cross-modality interaction patterns for protein-molecule virtual screening. The authors formalize a V-structure causal model under Heckman-style selection and prove three theoretical results on identifiability, then validate three implementation variants on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA benchmarks, reporting consistent gains over strong retrieval baselines, especially on LIT-PCBA early enrichment and out-of-distribution splits. Virtual screening is a core computational step in early drug discovery, and current representation-learning methods often overfit to nuisance correlations that fail to transfer to new protein targets. By grounding the learning objective in causal identifiability of sparse binding interactions, CausalBind offers a principled path toward models that generalize across targets and scaffolds, which could reduce costly late-stage screening failures. The paper establishes three theoretical results: latent concepts of interacting proteins and molecules are not identifiable without sparsity constraints, they become component-wise identifiable under structural sparsity, and a low-rank relaxation yields subspace identifiability. The paper introduces Lagrangian Responsibility Allocation (LiRA), a method that learns each agent's share of a common Lagrange multiplier by optimizing social welfare over a finite training horizon, rather than applying uniform or agent-specific penalties. Across CityLearn, MABIM, Harvest, and MetaDrive with 3 to 400 agents, LiRA improves average social welfare by up to 29% over uniform and agent-specific multiplier baselines while keeping grid and driving costs within budget. For convex games under standard regularity conditions, varying responsibility shares induces a smooth family of normalized generalized Nash equilibria where active constraints remain at their budgets while welfare varies. The authors derive a welfare gradient that accounts for both learning updates and the induced change in data distribution, enabling optimization of responsibility before convergence.

## [Dual-FDM disentangles dual image references via frequency-aware diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07684) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Dual-FDM, a frequency-aware diffusion model that disentangles dual image references (customization and color/style references) by manipulating frequency bands via mask strategies within the frequency domain. It tackles two personalized generation tasks—customization style transfer and color style transfer—by replacing mid-frequency bands for the former and low-frequency bands for the latter, using the substituted bands as key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background. This approach addresses a key limitation in personalized image generation where text misalignment occurs during denoising due to entangled frequency bands, potentially improving text alignment and generation quality for customization and style transfer tasks. It offers a more controllable and interpretable way to combine multiple references, which could benefit applications like virtual try-on, artistic rendering, and content creation. The model uses a mask strategy to disentangle frequency bands: for customization style transfer, it replaces the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference; for color style transfer, it substitutes the low-frequency band of the background with that from both foreground and background of the color reference. The substituted bands serve as key and value in attention to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised image.

Previous methods often entangle these bands when using multiple references, causing text misalignment. Dual-FDM separates these bands to better control which aspects of each reference are used.

## [WASD: Wasserstein-Based Knowledge Distillation for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07706) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers from KAIST's AI Lab proposed WASD, a knowledge distillation method for large language models that uses a Wasserstein-based distance with a cost matrix derived from token embeddings to capture token-level semantic information. To keep computation tractable, they adopt the Sinkhorn divergence and derive a gradient-equivalent objective that requires no additional networks, and experiments across multiple LLM families and scales show consistent improvements on instruction following, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Knowledge distillation is a key technique for compressing large models into smaller, cheaper ones for deployment, and WASD shows that incorporating semantic relationships between tokens—rather than only per-index probability values—can improve how well a student model learns from its teacher. This could lead to more capable small models for practical inference-constrained settings, though the impact is incremental within a specialized research area. The method replaces conventional divergences like KL that compare probability values at each vocabulary index with a Wasserstein distance whose cost matrix comes from token embeddings, and it uses the Sinkhorn divergence to make the optimal transport computation tractable. The authors derive a gradient-equivalent objective that avoids introducing extra networks, and the implementation is publicly available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher" model, typically by aligning their output probability distributions, which is a common way to reduce inference cost for large language models. The Wasserstein distance (also known as the earth mover's distance) measures the minimum cost of transforming one probability distribution into another over a metric space, and the Sinkhorn divergence is an entropy-regularized approximation that makes this computation efficient. Token embeddings are vector representations of vocabulary items that encode semantic similarity, so using them as a cost matrix lets the distillation loss account for how semantically close different tokens are.

## [TICDA: Fast Data Attribution for Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07996) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced TICDA, a method that measures the influence of each in-context demonstration on a tabular foundation model's prediction directly from linear surrogates trained on the model's latent embeddings, requiring only a single forward pass. The paper reports that TICDA outperforms competing attribution methods across four tasks: detecting labeling errors, curating context to cut inference cost while preserving accuracy, transferring attribution scores across different TFMs, and supporting an active-learning acquisition strategy. Tabular foundation models are increasingly used for zero-shot prediction on tabular data, but practitioners have had no cheap way to know which in-context examples help or hurt a prediction. TICDA gives a practical, low-cost tool for debugging mislabeled or redundant demonstrations and for shrinking context windows, which could make TFM deployment more reliable and cheaper. Standard attribution approaches do not transfer to this setting: resampling-based methods like DemoShapley need a combinatorial number of forward passes, while gradient-based influence functions assume parameter updates that in-context learning never performs. TICDA sidesteps both problems by working on latent embeddings with linear surrogates, though the abstract is truncated and full empirical details, such as dataset scale and baseline comparisons, are not yet visible.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Tabular foundation models are pretrained on large collections of mostly simulated datasets and make predictions by conditioning on labeled examples placed in the context, without any task-specific training. This in-context learning setup means the quality of the demonstrations directly shapes the output, yet the context is often assembled from whatever labeled data happens to be available. Data attribution aims to trace a prediction back to the specific examples responsible for it, a problem studied for years in classical machine learning via influence functions and Shapley-value methods.

## [Penalty-Framed No-Valid-Option MCQA Exposes LLM Abstention Gaps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08153) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08153) introduces penalty-framed no-valid-option MCQA, a setting in which the labeled correct option is removed from the mathematics subset of MMLU-Pro, models may either pick a remaining option or output ABSTAIN, and invalid forced-choice responses are penalized. The authors also propose correct-conditioned analysis, evaluating abstention only on instances the model originally answered correctly, and find that even with explicit no-valid-option instructions and penalty-based scoring, models still emit invalid forced-choice answers on a subset of those originally correct instances. The work shows that high multiple-choice accuracy does not guarantee reliable abstention, meaning standard answer-selection accuracy can hide a real reliability gap that matters in deployments where retrieval systems or users supply invalid option sets. This has implications for LLM evaluation practice and for safety-critical applications where silently picking a wrong option incurs downstream cost. The experiments use the mathematics subset of MMLU-Pro, a reasoning-centric benchmark that expands multiple-choice options from 4 to 10 and removes trivial questions, and the scoring explicitly penalizes invalid forced-choice responses rather than merely rewarding correct selections. The correct-conditioned analysis isolates abstention reliability from general question-answering ability by restricting evaluation to instances the model originally answered correctly.

## [FoG: Foresight-Aware Retrieval for Knowledge Base QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08388) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Foresight-over-Graph (FoG), a foresight-aware evidence retrieval framework for knowledge base question answering (KBQA) that uses far-to-near feedback to guide path exploration instead of hop-wise greedy or beam-style pruning. Experiments on widely used KBQA benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, including a 16.58% improvement in Hit on CWQ, while reducing LLM calls and token usage. This work addresses a known limitation in LLM-guided graph reasoning for KBQA: local pruning can prematurely discard evidence that only becomes relevant after deeper graph exploration. By improving retrieval foresight and reducing LLM calls, FoG could make knowledge-graph-grounded reasoning more reliable and cost-efficient for knowledge-intensive question answering. FoG iteratively constructs a question-relevant evidence subgraph and maintains a compact memory subgraph to support continued exploration, using far-to-near feedback to guide path exploration. The code is available at https://github.com/yhong7/FoG, and the approach is evaluated on standard KBQA benchmarks such as CWQ.

## [Probing Latent Unanswerability Signals Across Domains and Dialogue Turns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08413) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper introduces a turn-labeled multi-turn benchmark of 423 conversations and 1,661 labeled turn-states, plus an evaluation harness with a simulated user, to test how far probes for latent unanswerability generalize across six datasets and six open-weight LLMs. It finds that probes transfer robustly between datasets sharing a ground of unanswerability (math AUROC 0.77-0.97; SQuAD 2.0<->MuSiQue 0.77-0.90), but single-turn probes fail zero-shot to detect when a conversation becomes answerable. The work provides a reusable benchmark and harness for studying when LLMs should abstain or ask for clarification, a core problem for reducing hallucinations and improving dialogue reliability. It also shows that the remaining gap lies mostly in how models use a clarification rather than in detecting underspecification, pointing future research toward generation and consolidation rather than detection alone. Probes for epistemic "known-unknowns" transfer poorly to math, but this separation weakens under lexical controls and changes with layer and coordinate system, so it remains unresolved. A calibrated probe gate fires on underspecified turns far more precisely than chance and comes within 0.08 of a gate given true labels, yet across four models it does not reliably beat vanilla generation or prompted consolidation.

**Background**: Linear probing is a technique that trains a simple linear classifier on a model's internal hidden states to test whether a property, such as unanswerability, is linearly decodable from its representations. ## [Learning Style Shapes Unlearning: Generalization-Heavy Models Suffer More Retain Damage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08577) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08577) investigates how a model's learning strategy—memorization versus generalization—affects subsequent machine unlearning. Using grokking in modular addition to classify models, the authors find that generalization-heavy models experience greater retain damage, a trend that persists nearly monotonically across a controlled memorization-generalization spectrum and also holds in LLM unlearning for verbatim and factual recall. This work highlights that unlearning effectiveness is not independent of how a model learned, suggesting that future unlearning methods should account for training dynamics. It could influence the design of safer and more reliable unlearning algorithms, especially for large language models where removing sensitive or copyrighted content is increasingly important. The study uses grokking in modular addition to separate memorization- and generalization-heavy models, then introduces bucketed modular addition to explicitly control the contributions of each strategy. The same trend is reaffirmed in LLM unlearning across verbatim and factual recall settings, and the authors provide two practical insights for developing better unlearning methods.

## [MemFLoRA Cuts CNN Edge Adaptation Memory by Up to 98.7%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08669) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new paper introduces MemFLoRA, a memory-floor LoRA adapter for CNNs that freezes the down-projection, trains a scale-matched up-projection, and uses eval-mode backbone normalization with activation-minimal backward rules. Evaluated on three Human Activity Recognition datasets and two CNN backbones, it reduces saved-activation memory by 98.5-98.7% and peak training-state memory by 94.9-97.3% versus full fine-tuning while matching or exceeding CNN PEFT baselines. On-device learning is essential when deployed models face user-, sensor-, or environment-specific shifts, and this work shows that activation memory, not trainable parameter count, is the real bottleneck for CNN adaptation at the edge. By reframing LoRA design around a memory-first principle, it could make practical on-device fine-tuning feasible on resource-constrained hardware where full fine-tuning is impossible. The core criterion is an activation-memory-floor: trainable backward computations must not depend on full-width layer inputs, so saved state is reduced to the low-rank branch. The evaluation covers subject, body-location, and sensor-placement shifts, though results are limited to HAR tasks and CNN backbones rather than broader vision or transformer workloads.

## [Policy-Aware Selection Framework for Competing Uncertainty-Aware Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05479) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes a policy-aware framework for selecting among multiple uncertainty-aware explanations for the same prediction, balancing prediction confidence, uncertainty, and application constraints. It instantiates the framework with Calibrated Explanations for classification, thresholded regression, and plain regression, and evaluates it on 41 benchmark datasets, where mean candidate counts range from 11.57 to 21.75 for single-feature explanations and from 29.48 to 69.53 when conjunctions are included. As uncertainty-aware explanation methods increasingly produce multiple alternative explanations for a single prediction, practitioners need a principled way to choose among them rather than relying on ad hoc heuristics. By making the selection policy explicit, this framework allows applications to compare and prioritise explanations according to their intended use, which is important for trustworthy AI in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance. Candidates are characterised by uncertainty change, prediction direction, and, when available, interval position relative to a decision boundary; the framework combines these with eligibility rules, optional bidirectional Pareto screening, and policy-aware ranking. Equal-weight and confidence-only policies yield an average selection-disagreement rate of 28.7% while favouring the same confidence direction, and a supporting δ-CLUE experiment demonstrates use with a second generator.

## [Reward on Path: Learning Intermediate Supervision for KGQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10791) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes Reward on Path (RoP), a framework that learns a lightweight, question-conditioned path reward from answer labels using an asymmetric objective, then uses it to train an LLM-based relation path generator in two stages: reward distillation and on-policy GRPO optimization. Experiments on multiple KGQA datasets show RoP improves F1 over answer-derived methods by at least 2.6% while outperforming LLM-refined methods without costly supervision construction. This work addresses a core bottleneck in KGQA: answer-derived supervision treats every answer-reaching path as correct, producing noisy training signals, while LLM-refined supervision is costly. By learning a lightweight reward model that distinguishes path quality, RoP offers a cheaper and cleaner alternative that could improve how LLM-based reasoning systems retrieve evidence from knowledge graphs. RoP supervises paths reaching the same answer jointly as a bag so the reward model can learn their relative contributions, while penalizing each path individually for retrieving non-answer entities. The learned reward is transferred to the generator via reward distillation and further refined with GRPO on self-generated paths, and generated paths are grounded in the KG to retrieve evidence for answer reasoning.

## [TwinCheck Verifies Tool Calls via Negative-Twin Counterfactuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26911) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TwinCheck introduces an inference-time verification policy that only replaces an agent's proposed tool call when the trace satisfies an evidence condition tied to a trace-local failure hypothesis, and a constructed counterfactual alternative (the "negative twin") passes structural checks and is preferred by a pairwise verifier in both candidate orders. On 159 multi-turn BFCL V4 tasks with complete exact-replay pairs, the full policy raised task success for GPT-5.6 Sol from 45.3% to 58.5% (95% task-bootstrap CI [8.2, 18.8]) with no observed success-to-failure regressions. A single locally plausible but harmful tool call can derail an otherwise successful agent trajectory, so this work reframes execution-boundary repair as a constrained comparison where the counterfactual action itself is verified rather than blindly substituted. It matters for developers building stateful tool-using agents, since it offers an inference-time reliability improvement without retraining the underlying model. The paired evaluation uses exact replay to hold the agent's parsed responses and actions fixed until the first accepted replacement, which separates intervention effects from resampling noise. The reported gains come from a primary analysis of 159 multi-turn BFCL V4 tasks with complete exact-replay pairs, and the abstract notes no observed success-to-failure regressions.

## [Finite-Sample Prediction Bounds for Soft State Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32652) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper derives a finite-sample lower confidence bound on the smallest population root-mean-square prediction error achievable by any linear predictor with a bounded spectral norm, for a fixed soft state representation whose nonnegative class weights sum to one. The bound is computed directly from independent evaluation pairs without fitting a prediction matrix, and is validated on a four-state study across 117,000 replicate datasets plus a Van der Pol representation tested on 32 independent datasets under two transition laws. This work gives practitioners a way to certify, before training any predictor, whether a chosen representation can possibly achieve a desired accuracy, which is valuable for representation learning and Koopman-based dynamical systems modeling. It also clarifies the distinction between agreement with reconstruction classes, attainable prediction accuracy, and exact operator closure. A bound above a chosen tolerance rules out that tolerance for the entire matrix class, but a zero bound is inconclusive; for Kernel Affine Hull Machine coordinates, reconstruction-score margins control disagreement with reference labels and feed into the prediction-error bounds. The reported bounds are positive at the fitted matrix norm but can shrink to zero at larger norm limits, and the paper also establishes a Koopman and reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space adjoint interpretation under exact deterministic linear evolution, accounting for redundant coefficient vectors.

## [BORF: A Fast, Interpretable, Deterministic Time Series Classifier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.18029) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes Bag-Of-Receptive-Field (BORF), a time series transform that enhances the classical Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAX) with dilation and stride, and introduces an algorithmic speedup that reduces the time complexity of SAX-based classifiers. Tested on more than 150 univariate and multivariate classification datasets, BORF achieves good accuracy and strong computational efficiency compared to traditional SAX-based methods and state-of-the-art time series classifiers while providing human-understandable explanations. Most state-of-the-art time series classifiers are black-box ensemble hybrids that prioritize predictive performance over transparency, and even supposedly interpretable shapelet-based methods rely on randomization that makes explanations unstable across runs. BORF addresses this gap by offering a deterministic transform that is simultaneously accurate, efficient, and interpretable, which matters for high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance where reproducible explanations are essential. BORF extends the Bag-Of-Patterns paradigm to a more flexible Bag-Of-Receptive-Fields representation stored as a sparse multivariate tensor, bridging convolutional operators and discretization to capture temporal patterns at multiple scales. The key technical contribution is an algorithmic speedup that lowers the time complexity of SAX-based classification, enabling the extension to dilation and stride without prohibitive cost.

SAX discretizes a time series into symbolic strings, but standard SAX lacks dilation and stride, limiting its ability to capture patterns at multiple temporal scales. Interpretability in machine learning refers to the degree to which a human can understand the cause of a model's decision, and deterministic algorithms always produce the same output for the same input, unlike randomized methods.

Guided diffusion sampling adds a segmentation-consistency loss and a class-wise feature matching loss, and code is available on GitHub.

## [Multi-Scale Features Boost Gradient-Free Continual Visual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25531) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a new multi-scale visual feature representation that encodes edge and contour structure together with their spatial relations, integrated into a developmental, gradient-free learning framework. Tested on class-incremental MNIST, it substantially improves shape recognition accuracy over the prior representation while preserving the framework's continual-learning guarantee and human-interpretable internal structure. It shows that continual learning without replay buffers or task boundaries can match or exceed replay- and regularization-based baselines at comparable storage, offering an alternative to gradient-based deep learning for settings where retention and interpretability matter. This could influence research on lifelong learning, robotics, and any system that must learn from a non-stationary stream of data. The work targets two-dimensional shape recognition with class-incremental MNIST as a controlled benchmark, and the key differentiator is retention: baselines surrender most of a just-trained class within its own cycle and relearn it later, whereas this method does not. The framework learns one sample at a time and provably preserves responses to earlier inputs without destructive adaptation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Continual learning aims to let models acquire new knowledge over time without catastrophically forgetting what they already learned; most deep learning methods rely on gradient descent plus replay buffers or regularization to approximate this. Developmental, gradient-free learning instead builds a discrete, topological model of inputs through local variation and selection, which inherently avoids overwriting past structure. Multi-scale representations, such as image pyramids, capture features at several resolutions, which helps encode both fine edges and broader contours.

A new arXiv paper (2607.26368v3) benchmarks frozen encoders, fine-tuned encoders, evidence-augmented classifiers, prompted LLMs, and LoRA-adapted generative models on the synthetic SBID-FD benchmark for classifying 11 types of inconsistencies in financial disclosure text. It finds that task-specific adaptation yields large gains over frozen representations, and a fine-tuned 300M encoder performs competitively with substantially larger prompted and adapted models. The study uses a fixed snapshot of the synthetic SBID-FD benchmark and a shared evaluation protocol across all model families. It further tests matched predicted-span, reference-span, and distractor-span conditions, finding that automatically extracted evidence adds signal but recovers only part of the benefit from reference spans, and that some inconsistency types are especially sensitive to localization quality while others remain hard even with relevant evidence.

## [Benchmark Evaluates LLM Agent Planning in Cyber-Physical Power Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04265) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2608.04265v2) introduces a controlled benchmark that evaluates planning-induced control trajectories of LLM agents in strategic cyber-physical systems, using four coded executors (predefined, sequential, hierarchical, and search) to manage demand response for 40 prosumers on a radial feeder. Experiments with Llama-3.3-70B show that forced search acts as the oracle across five baseline seeds, while injected objective substitution preserves mode agreement at 1.0 but increases cumulative voltage shortfall by 2.68x. This work shifts LLM-agent evaluation from simple task success to whether an architecture remains appropriate after autonomous participants respond and physical constraints bind, which matters for deploying LLM agents in power grids and other safety-critical cyber-physical systems. It offers a rigorous methodology—paired counterfactuals, exact-prompt caching, and event-level feasibility—that other researchers can reuse to test planning strategies under strategic interaction. The 144-scenario, 576-episode factorial bank with three repeated seeds contains feasible oracles from predefined, sequential, and search executors; a prespecified stress-held-out ridge has mean regret 90.7 with no observed value over fixed sequential, and a post-hoc constraint-aware analysis reduces regret to 29.0 while a simple deadline rule attains 28.7, so no learning advantage is established. The authors stress these are simulation-internal, descriptive comparisons, and a five-model, 300-declaration extension tests interface behaviour rather than cross-backbone physical rankings.

## [Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy Framework Diagnoses Prompt Injection Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26423) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2608.26423v2) introduces the Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy, a framework that builds dimensionality-optimized classifiers and adds a diagnostic layer to identify which confident decisions can be trusted. Applied to a public prompt injection dataset, it finds that about 77% of the classifier's confident decisions are not robust to removing a single token, splitting this brittleness into a confidence calibration failure and a genuinely exploitable shortcut. Prompt injection is a major security risk for LLM-based applications, and classifiers are often deployed as safeguard layers whose confident outputs are assumed correct. This work shows that most confident decisions can be flipped by a single token, and offers a taxonomy to flag which prompts need human review, which could change how AI security teams validate and trust guardrail models. The framework selects embedding dimensionality empirically via cross-validated performance rather than fixing it a priori, and locates a small set of latent support vectors (~29% of training examples) whose tokens can alter predicted labels. It then sorts prompts into four zones: rely Safely, flag Heuristic Bias, flag Heuristic Override, and route Insufficient Context for human or safety review, with remediation strategies recommended for each zone.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 8, 04:00

**Background**: Prompt injection is a cybersecurity exploit in which crafted inputs cause a machine learning model, especially a large language model, to follow unintended instructions and bypass safeguards. Classifiers are often trained on prompt datasets and used as a safeguard layer to detect such attacks. Support vector machines are supervised max-margin models that classify data by finding a separating hyperplane, and support vectors are the influential training examples that define that boundary. Embedding dimensionality is the size of the vector representation of text, and it is usually chosen by the user or tuned through cross-validation.

## [CSWAM adds V-JEPA 2.1 causal expert to FastWAM for OOD generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18462) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CSWAM augments FastWAM-style world action models with a causal semantic expert built on V-JEPA 2.1, which learns temporally grounded representations of semantic state changes and motion from a sparse history of current and past observations. With embodied pretraining, CSWAM raises Randomized success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Randomized transfer from 10.16% to 45.18% (a 35.02 percentage point gain over FastWAM), and improves average success across two real-robot tasks and three OOD difficulty levels by 42.5 percentage points, from 27.5% to 70.0%. Out-of-distribution generalization under visual distribution shifts is a core bottleneck for deploying world action models in real embodied settings, where lighting, textures, and object appearances rarely match training data. CSWAM's large empirical gains on both simulation and real robots suggest that injecting self-supervised video semantics into action models could make robot policies substantially more robust without sacrificing efficient action-only inference. CSWAM shares history-derived context with both the video and action streams through causal attention, and at inference conditions action denoising on the current video state plus observed semantic history while retaining efficient action-only inference. The reported gains depend on embodied pretraining, and the paper is an arXiv preprint with no code release mentioned.

## [NormPaST-Risk Detects Alzheimer's via Handwriting Segments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29384) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces NormPaST-Risk, a healthy-normative Paper-Air selective trajectory state-space risk network that reformulates online handwriting-based Alzheimer's disease detection as local disease-relevant segment discovery rather than whole-trajectory classification. It combines a multi-scale temporal encoder, a selective Paper-Air state-space encoder, a healthy normative branch, and a task-aware multi-expert segment-risk module, achieving superior AD/HC classification on the DARWIN benchmark while projecting high-risk segments back onto the original handwriting trajectory for interpretability. This work could make Alzheimer's screening cheaper and more accessible, since online handwriting is a non-invasive, low-cost behavioral biomarker that can be captured with a digital pen or tablet. By pinpointing which local handwriting segments carry disease signal, it also addresses a key weakness of global-feature methods that are confounded by individual writing style, task variation, and acquisition noise. The method uses a weakly supervised segment-level objective to discover high-risk segments without manual segment annotations, and the selective Paper-Air state-space encoder explicitly separates on-paper motor execution from in-air planning and transition behavior. Evaluation is limited to the DARWIN benchmark, and the abstract does not report specific accuracy numbers or cross-dataset generalization results.

A new arXiv paper (2610.02659v2) derives architecture-aware gradient and smoothness bounds for single- and multi-layer selective state space models such as Mamba2, and uses them to obtain convergence bounds for FedAvg and FedProx. The authors numerically validate the single-layer bounds on teacher-generated sequences and then compare nine federated learning algorithms on Mamba2 language modeling across six text domains. Existing federated learning methods are largely architecture-agnostic, so this work is among the first to explain how SSM-specific properties such as recurrent stability and input-dependent discretization shape federated optimization. It could guide the design of more effective distributed training schemes as Mamba-style models gain traction as linear-time alternatives to transformers. The bounds explicitly characterize how recurrent stability, input-dependent discretization, and state projection norms affect federated optimization, and the analysis is used to form expectations about local training and client heterogeneity. ## [Local2Mesh reconstructs 3D left ventricle from sparse 2D cardiac MRI contours](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06052) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Local2Mesh introduces a spatially localized contour-to-mesh framework that deforms a template mesh to reconstruct 3D left ventricular geometry from sparse 2D cardiac MRI contours without requiring 3D mesh annotations. It combines geometry-aware alignment to correct inter-slice misalignment with a plane-aware Local Router that routes contour features to template vertices using vertex-to-plane distances, and it outperforms existing methods on the M&Ms-2 and ACDC datasets. Sparse 2D short-axis cardiac MRI slices are the clinical standard, but reconstructing accurate 3D left ventricular shape from them is difficult; a method that works without 3D mesh annotations could make 3D cardiac analysis more practical. The paper also shows that reconstructed meshes improve downstream disease classification over sparse contours, suggesting value for clinical cardiac assessment. The framework uses local and global contour features jointly to guide graph-based template deformation, and zero-shot transfer from M&Ms-2 to ACDC demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/hwu918945-alt/loca2mesh, though the approach is a specialized incremental advance rather than a paradigm shift.

**Background**: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is the reference standard for quantitative assessment of cardiac structure and function, and cine CMR typically covers the left ventricle with a stack of 2D short-axis slices plus long-axis views. Because these slices are sparse, there is insufficient local spatial information between them and inter-slice misalignment can occur, making 3D reconstruction challenging. Template mesh deformation is a common approach in medical imaging, where a template mesh is deformed to match anatomical shapes in a 3D scan, but global aggregation of contour features may obscure local contour-to-surface relationships.
